title: Phantom-Load Registry: Land Records Meet Utility Queues
one_liner: A utility-funded vetting desk that joins courthouse land-assembly signals with co-op and municipal large-load inquiry logs, so it can say which 100-1,000 MW projects are real and which LLC families are shopping the same megawatts to five utilities.
customer: Electric co-ops, G&Ts, municipal utilities and PUDs with 5-person engineering staffs. They pay per memo or on retainer. Secondary buyers are developers' land teams and site-selection consultants, infrastructure and energy funds buying alt-data, and county economic-development offices.
problem: Every party sees half the picture. A small utility sees the inquiry (an LLC, a MW ask, a PowerPoint) but not the land trail. The land-assembly watcher sees option memoranda and easements but cannot tell a real hyperscale campus from a speculator flipping dirt. Nobody sees the same MW shopped across states. Texas SB 6's collateral rule (final expected by end of 2026) will push phantom load onto softer neighbors.
solution: First product is the fixed-price vetting memo ($7.5-25k) with a red/amber/green result and a recommended security amount. The site-control and LLC-principal items in the 12-point physical-reality test are powered by an image-level read of recorded options, leases and easements, clustered by return-to law firm, notary, signatory and mailing address. Air-permit and equipment-slot checks come from the vetting desk. Utilities that share their inquiry logs (LLC, MW, node, date, outcome) get discounted memos. Those logs become a multi-utility duplicate-request registry that flags land-assembled-but-no-equipment-slot projects and the same LLC family filing at several utilities. Later products are a county-level real-versus-phantom alert feed and alt-data licenses for funds.
why_now: Texas SB 6 (PUCT rule final due by 12/31/2026, $50,000/MW security) is exporting speculators to neighboring states. About half of announced 2026 builds are delayed or cancelled, so utilities are burned and skeptical. FinCEN's 2025 exemption for domestic companies means LLC unmasking has to come from primary records. LLM vision now reads messy scanned instruments accurately.
revenue_model: $7.5-25k per vetting memo. $60-150k per year G&T retainers. $2-8k per month regional developer seats. $750-2,000 per tract title packet. $50-150k per year alt-data licenses for funds. Utilities often pass memo cost to applicants as a study-deposit line item. Later, registry subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Land records show intent, and an option memo is cheap to buy. The equipment and permit trail shows capability. The utility queue shows the ask. No single dataset separates real from speculative, but the join does. Land assembled with no transformer slot, by an LLC family filing at five utilities, is a land flip. Each utility's eventual outcome (built, cancelled, withdrawn) is also a free labeled training set for the tape's classifier, which no scraper competitor can get. Utilities will only share inquiry logs with someone they already trust to vet, and that is a trust position a pure data vendor lacks.
first_30_days: Through state electric cooperative associations, get 3 co-ops to hand over their last 10 inquiries each. Pull 24 months of recorded instruments in those territories, plus state air-permit and LLC filings. Run a free back-test showing which past inquiries were real. Publish a '12 signs your data center inquiry is real' one-pager and send a sample 'who is assembling where' memo to 10 site-selection consultants. Convert 2-3 co-ops to paid $7.5k memos on live inquiries and pitch one G&T retainer.
lineage: hybrid of I0773 + I0079 (Courthouse Tape: Land-Assembly Radar for Infrastructure + Phantom Load Vetting Desk for Rural Utilities). Why stronger: The vetting desk alone is a services business with a thin data moat, and the tape alone fights for alt-data budgets with no ground-truth labels. Together, memo revenue funds data collection, utility outcomes label the data, and the pooled duplicate registry gets more valuable with each utility that joins. ACV rises, and utilities can be reached through co-op associations instead of cold outreach.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ATTOM Data, Reonomy, Regrid, Enverus. White space: The specific product in the idea, a feed that reads recorded option memoranda, leases and easements from county recorders, classifies them from the image rather than the clerk's label, clusters LLC families by notary, return-to firm and address, and alerts on assembly patterns, was not found at any vendor I could read. Everything I could read is adjacent. Parcel and ownership vendors (Regrid, ATTOM, Reonomy) sell deeds, mortgages and LLC piercing but not options or easements. Siting and diligence vendors (Paces, Enverus, GridCARE) help a client find its own site. Project trackers (Cleanview, DC Byte, Heatmap Pro, Data Center Watch) start at permit or public news. Land-management vendors (Pandell, Enverus LandScape) manage a client's own documents. What remains open is cross-county, image-level reading of recorded non-deed instruments to detect other parties' assembly, sold as alerts. It is plausibly protected by the hard part, which is getting recorder access county by county, not the ML. The main structural doubts I could not test are whether developers actually record option memoranda before announcement, and how many counties allow bulk commercial pulls of document images. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GridUnity, Clean Power Research (PowerClerk), Enverus, LandGate. White space: I found no direct competitor. No startup, consultancy or association was selling a utility-side, per-inquiry 'is this developer physically real' memo with a recommended collateral amount and milestone-gated study structure. The gap is real but narrow.

What is unserved: (1) External physical-trail verification for small utilities, meaning air-permit generator counts vs claimed MW, recorded deeds and options, LLC principal cross-checks, and OEM or EPC evidence. GridUnity and PowerClerk track applicant-supplied data but do not verify it. Enverus, LandGate and GridCARE serve the developer side. (2) A cross-utility duplicate-request registry. Texas SB 6 mandates duplicate-request disclosure only inside ERCOT. Outside ERCOT there is no pooled registry. Developers do file the same project with several utilities (Latitude Media, Utility Dive). (3) Packaging for 5-person co-op engineering staffs: I found no NRECA vetting checklist or tool, and no small-utility-specific vendor.

Serious weaknesses the founder must address:
- Regulation and tariffs are substituting for vetting. Collateral, study fees and site-control mandates make the applicant self-prove. Exelon cut its estimates about 40% after stricter collateral. AEP Ohio's pipeline fell by more than half after study fees of up to $100K (https://techstartups.com/2026/09/01/ai-data-centers-request-700-gw-of-u-s-power-but-much-of-the-demand-may-be-an-illusion/). Once a co-op requires a deposit, site control and a signed LOI, much of the 12-point test becomes documents the applicant hands over.
- Texas SB 6 / 16 TAC 25.194 applies only in ERCOT (https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/03/texas-proposes-new-interconnection-standards-for-large-electric-loads). The 'small utilities in neighboring states get the displaced phantoms' claim is plausible but I found no evidence for it.
- Several tests may not be observable by an outsider. OEM order acknowledgments and financing letters are confidential, and real developers often approach the utility before ordering equipment.
- Regulators are absorbing the LLC-transparency piece. Texas ordered an audit requiring true-ownership disclosure, and Pennsylvania issued an August 18 executive order for projects over 25 MW.
- Big engineering consultancies could add this as a service line. I could not verify whether they already do. My web-search budget ran out before I could check.

title: Ship-Date Cliff Audits for Phased Campuses
one_liner: A fixed-fee clock-map, rider-negotiation and proof-test sprint for developers of multi-phase data center campuses whose pre-bought gensets, UPS and chillers were shipped long before the halls they serve, so the OEM 18-months-from-ship outer limit expires before startup.
customer: Wedge buyer: the VP of procurement or construction director at colo developers and neoclouds building multi-phase campuses (100MW+, with phases 2-4 not yet energized) that accepted long-lead MEP deliveries ahead of the shell. Start with generators, then UPS. Secondary buyer: the lender's technical advisor asking for an equipment warranty schedule at draw or refinancing.
problem: The judges and the competitor check both found that the parent's premise is too broad. Startup plus load-bank IST already loads most equipment, so the 'idle hall' exposure is narrow. The clean exposure is different. OEM terms run to the earlier of about 12 months from startup or 18 months from factory ship (Cummins, Eaton and Trane terms in the research). Developers buy gear in blocks for phases 2-4 to lock lead-time slots and pre-tariff prices, and take delivery into yards or spare rooms. When a phase slips, the outer limit lapses before the unit is ever started. Storage voiding conditions (heaters, battery freshening charges, engine exercise) are usually undocumented, so an OEM can also deny on those grounds. Procurement has moved on, the ship date lives in a bill of lading nobody rereads, and ops inherits the unit with no idea the clock ran out.
solution: 1) Cliff calendar. Per serial number, extract ship date (bill of lading, delivery ticket), planned startup, outer-limit date and voiding conditions. The LLM pipeline is an internal tool; the deliverable is a one-page dated list of cliffs. 2) Rider sprint. Before each cliff, negotiate a written start-date deferral or delayed-start rider with the OEM. Package it campus-wide, because the owner's phase 3-4 orders are the leverage a single-unit rider buyer lacks. 3) Storage-compliance repair. Fix missing exercise, heater and battery-charge logs so the OEM loses its easy denial grounds. 4) Proof test. For installed units 6-9 months before the cliff, run a staged load test using a load-bank rental partner, then file claims with OEM-grade evidence while the OEM is still liable. Contingency is not the lead model.
why_now: Long-lead power gear (gensets, transformers, switchgear) is being bought years ahead of buildings, and phase slippage is widespread in 2026 reporting. Tariffs make each unit more expensive, so each lapsed warranty is worth more. LLMs make serial-level extraction from delivery documents cheap. Delayed-start riders exist (Trane), so the ask is normal to OEMs but rarely made.
revenue_model: $30-60K fixed fee per campus phase for the cliff calendar plus rider negotiation. $60-120K per year campus retainer that keeps the calendar live as phases progress. Load-test pass-through with a 15% markup, plus a referral fee from the rental partner. Success fee of 20% of OEM-accepted claim value, measured by the OEM's claim number or credit memo, and 10% of the discount won on riders versus list. Assumption to validate: about 30 campus programs at roughly $80K per year is about $2.4M ARR with 2-3 people.
non_obvious_insight: The exposed population is defined by shipment date versus startup date, not by whether a hall is idle. That makes it provable from documents and public filings before any owner talks to you. It also makes the contingency-collection problem disappear: a signed deferral or an OEM credit memo is a countable outcome, unlike 'avoided repair cost'. The leverage is future orders across the campus, which the owner has and a one-off rider purchase does not.
first_30_days: Build a target list from public state air-permit filings for backup diesel generators, which typically list unit counts and models by phase, cross-referenced with press releases and county filings. Rank 40 campuses where permitted units far exceed operating ones. Email the procurement lead a one-page teaser: 'if your gensets shipped in Q3 2025, the OEM outer limit lands in Q1 2027'. Land three owners who hand over POs and delivery tickets for a free 5-day clock map. Use the first dated cliff to open a rider conversation with the OEM before any invoice. This also answers the parent's unresolved question of whether clocks are truly running out on unstarted equipment.
lineage: mutation of I0229 ('Warranty Clock Recovery Audits for Idle Halls'), type: sharpened
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ethyco (data center commissioning, warranty-phase support), Anyset AI (agentic closeout / warranty tracking), Nomic (AEC document AI, closeout), Trane delayed start-up warranty (OEM rider). White space: Nobody I found combines all of these for data center MEP: (1) a serial-number-level clock ledger built for idle or deferred-start halls, (2) a pre-expiry loaded stress test using the idle capacity, (3) OEM claim filing and start-date deferral negotiation, and (4) success-fee or fixed-fee pricing sold to the owner or its lender. The pieces exist separately. Anyset and Nomic do doc extraction. Ethyco-style Cx firms do a 10-month warranty review. Wind and solar have end-of-warranty inspection and claims firms. OEMs sell delayed-start riders. Load-bank vendors have the hardware. Data center power and cooling MEP has no dedicated end-of-warranty claims specialist that I could find. Three structural weaknesses limit the wedge. (a) The clocks mostly start at OEM startup, and startup plus IST with load banks already loads equipment in Cx, so the 'idle for 12+ months' exposure is narrower than the pitch implies. It mainly hits gear started early or shipped more than 18 months before use. (b) 'Recovered value' is really avoided repair cost. It is hard to measure and easy for OEMs to dispute, and OEMs can deny on storage or light-load grounds (wet stacking is explicitly excluded, https://cliffordpower.com/wet-stacking-why-its-important-to-load-bank-your-diesel-generator/). A pure 25-30% contingency model will be hard to collect. (c) Documents are the commodity step, so the moat has to be inspection plus OEM leverage, not the LLM pipeline. | How this version avoids them: Ethyco and other Cx firms start their 10-month review after occupancy, so they sell to Cx and ops. This sells earlier, to procurement, and starts at shipment; it can also be white-labeled to them. Anyset, Nomic and Equipment Warranty Log commoditize extraction and stop at the ledger, so extraction is hidden here and the product is a dated outcome (signed deferral, accepted claim). Trane's delayed-start rider is a per-unit list product; a campus-wide negotiated deferral backed by future orders is not, and the rider becomes an input this business brokers. Wind, PV and BESS players (SGS, Sinovoltaics, TWAICE) serve other asset classes. CxPlanner and Bluerithm own punch lists, not shipment dates. Aggreko and Sunbelt Solomon are suppliers and referrers, not rivals. The judges' contingency-collection flaw is removed by leading with a fixed fee.

title: Orphan Fleet Depot for Bankrupt-Maker Electric Buses
one_liner: Sustainment-as-a-service for school districts and transit agencies stuck with electric buses whose manufacturer went bankrupt, using the military's orphan-platform playbook (salvaged parts pool, configuration control, depot repair, availability guarantees).
customer: School districts, regional education service agencies and small transit agencies that own buses from failed OEMs (Lion Electric US buses, Proterra, and similar EV truck and bus makers), plus state grant administrators and cooperative-purchasing bodies that want the taxpayer-funded fleets running.
problem: When Lion Electric went through bankruptcy and its new owner voided prior U.S. warranties, districts were left with buses nobody would service. Some sourced parts themselves, some sidelined buses, and some went back to diesel. Proterra's transit business went through a similar handoff. Grant-funded buses that sit idle are a political and audit embarrassment. Dealers cannot fix proprietary battery, inverter and charge-port faults, and there is no parts channel.
solution: Run it like a military orphan-platform sustainment program. (1) Buy the bankruptcy estate's remaining parts, tooling and diagnostics at liquidation. (2) Build a per-VIN configuration database and a reverse-engineered diagnostic library. (3) Stand up a regional depot and a mobile repair van for line-replaceable units: contactors, DC-DC converters, charge ports, battery management modules and pack modules. (4) Buy sidelined orphan buses cheaply as cannibalization donors. (5) Sell a fixed annual sustainment contract per bus that guarantees a morning-route availability rate, backed by a shared spares pool across districts sized with readiness-based sparing math.
why_now: Lion's sale voided U.S. warranties (reported late 2025), so the 2025-26 school year is when the pain became real. The installed base of grant-funded EV buses is large and aging out of warranty, and subsidy rollbacks (the federal commercial clean vehicle credit ended for vehicles acquired after Sept 30, 2025) make further OEM failures likely. The parts estates of failed makers are cheapest to buy right now, before anyone else sees their value.
revenue_model: Annual sustainment contract of roughly $4-8k per bus with an availability guarantee, plus time-and-materials for depot repairs, spares-pool membership fees for districts that want priority access, and salvage and refurbished battery pack sales. Sold through cooperative purchasing vehicles so districts do not each run a bid.
non_obvious_insight: Orphaned does not mean unfixable. In most orphaned fleets, 5-10 recurring line-replaceable units cause most of the downtime. A small shared spares pool plus a configuration-controlled baseline can lift availability from a coin flip to about 90%. The right buyer is not one district's bus garage but a state agency or regional service center pooling many districts, because the sparing math only works at fleet-of-fleets scale. Military sustainers call this the DMSMS problem and solved it by owning the baseline instead of waiting for the OEM.
first_30_days: Build a list of about 20 districts that took Lion or similar deliveries in 2022-24 from press coverage and grant award lists. Offer one district a free 'orphan health check' on a stranded bus using generic diagnostic tools and an EV-experienced transit mechanic. Register as a bidder in the relevant bankruptcy and liquidation processes and ask for the parts inventory lists. Hire 1-2 retired transit or heavy-duty EV technicians. Sign three districts to a per-bus quarterly pilot and use their fault logs to identify the top recurring failure modes.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Highland Electric Fleets, Hyroad Energy, Phoenix Motor (Phoenix Motorcars) / Proterra transit, Lion Bus (post-bankruptcy Lion Electric). White space: Not found in this research: any player selling a brand-agnostic, per-bus sustainment contract with an availability guarantee and a pooled spares inventory for orphaned electric school buses. Highland offers a guarantee for buses it deploys and Hyroad does the estate-buying for hydrogen trucks, but neither was found serving orphaned Lion buses. Herscher CUSD (IL), Winthrop (MA) and Yarmouth (ME) are paying ad hoc 'alternate vendors' or have parked buses, and the Electrek piece names no third-party service provider. The wedge is Lion's US-orphaned school buses. That is a small installed base, described only as 'dozens of districts', and its sizing was not verified. Multi-district pooling through a state agency or regional service center is also unserved. Caveats: this verdict comes from a thin evidence base, because the WebSearch budget ran out (200 of 200) and only about a dozen direct page fetches worked. No search of Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or open-source tools was possible. Small independent EV repair shops, dealers or school-bus contractors may already do this informally and would not show up in homepage fetches. Weaknesses in the idea: (a) the 'buy the estate cheaply now' premise looks partly stale, since Lion's US facilities were divested by mid-2025 and its Chapter 15 dates to Dec 2024, so the parts and tooling may already be sold; (b) Proterra transit has a successor OEM in Phoenix Motor; (c) battery, BMS and inverter repair on reverse-engineered buses carries fire and liability risk, given the EPA investigation of Lion bus fires and Quebec pulling Lion buses out of service; (d) the buyer pool is small and public budgets are slow.

title: Franchisee Flight Recorder and Recommendation Index
one_liner: Invert the advisor into a witness: a silent, tamper-evident ledger that records what the franchisor's AI recommended, what the owner ordered and what was binned, prices the gap under the owner's own contract, and scales into a franchisee-owned registry and a published Recommendation Cost Index for each chain.
customer: Start with legacy-contract Seven-Eleven owners in Kansai who fear OFC retaliation and will not use a tool that changes how they order. Then a franchisee-owned business cooperative, franchise-specialist law firms, lenders and analysts as data buyers, then regulators and convenience-store review panels as consumers of the aggregate. Later, Lawson and FamilyMart, Korea and Taiwan convenience chains, and other franchise systems with mandated promos, ordering or capex.
problem: The parent's insight stands: HQ recommendations optimize HQ's payoff. But advice tools stall on the owner's fear of the OFC, on HQ markdown pushes that commoditize the advice, and on Seven's new contract that shrinks the gap for new stores. Meanwhile owners have no evidence in the moments that matter: renewal or non-renewal talks, disputes about mismanagement, store sales, and any complaint to the JFTC or a METI panel. HQ holds the only record of what its AI recommended. The 2009 JFTC order on Seven-Eleven Japan and the Diamond and Toyo Keizai reporting show that regulators and press act on documented owner constraints, but individual owners hold anecdotes and one store is not statistics.
solution: Owner does nothing differently. Each day a LINE bot takes 3 photos or a forwarded CSV (the HQ order proposal screen, the order as placed, the disposal scan), extracts the data, and writes hashed records to a certified third-party time-stamp so the log is tamper-evident. The owner sees only a private monthly Ledger Statement: 'following HQ's proposals cost you X yen versus the optimum under your contract this month, Y yen cumulative', with no instruction and no OFC-visible change. The ledger is exported only on the owner's command to a lawyer, accountant, buyer or bank. Owners join a franchisee cooperative whose dues also fund a group-rate franchise-law retainer. Aggregated and anonymized across stores, the ledger yields per-item demand models that improve with store count and a quarterly Recommendation Cost Index for each chain, published as a neutral registry that regulators, lenders and press can cite. Every contract change (such as the 2027 Seven terms) becomes a natural experiment the index measures.
why_now: HQ AI ordering became the default at all three chains between 2023 and 2026, so a recorded 'recommended versus ordered versus binned' history now exists to capture. The disposal-share change in Seven's June 2026 contract shows HQ has conceded the conflict, and the METI convenience-store review panel is active. The 1 Oct 2026 wage step in Osaka makes every wasted yen hurt more. Photo OCR and structured extraction make daily capture cost pennies, and certified time-stamping is standard infrastructure. The outcome of the 2023 union case (loss at the Supreme Court) shows that collective action needs a data and legal structure other than a labor union, which a cooperative can supply.
revenue_model: 1,980 yen per store per month from owners (about the price of consumer legal-expense insurance, an assumption to verify), with the cooperative dues bundled. Case packs for law firms at 300,000 to 500,000 yen with an expert declaration, optionally a contingency share where the law firm agrees. Annual data licenses to lenders, analysts and research bodies (roughly 3M to 10M yen each). At 15% of about 55,000 stores subscribing that is roughly 200M yen a year from owners alone, before case packs, licenses and other chains or countries. The registry and index are the longer-term standard-setting asset.
non_obvious_insight: The fear that blocks the advice product is the buying reason for the recorder. An owner who will never argue with the OFC will still pay a small fee for a private ledger he never has to show. The value is a network good: one owner's log is an anecdote, but thousands of timestamped logs are the only regulator-grade evidence that a franchisor's recommendations systematically diverge from franchisee payoff, and they cannot be replicated by anyone who lacks owner trust. Because it gives no advice it does not compete with HQ AI on accuracy and is immune to markdown-push commoditization, and it stays useful under any contract terms, including the 50/50 one where a gap remains (owner critical ratio about 36% versus HQ's about 70%).
first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the LINE bot and ledger on the founder's three stores (the first real evidence file) and commission a one-week franchise-lawyer memo on data ownership and confidentiality plus the business-cooperative structure. Days 10-30: pre-sell 30 owners at 1,980 yen per month for 12 months via Kansai owner LINE and Facebook groups and 2 franchise-focused law firms, pitching it as 'a private record you never have to show anyone unless you need it'. Get one law firm to agree to a case-pack pilot price. Kill signals: fewer than 10 of 30 pre-sales, or the lawyer memo finds the HQ proposal screen cannot be recorded. Publish a one-page description of the Ledger Statement format and the planned index method to seed owner-to-owner sharing.
lineage: mutation of I0272 ('Owner-Side Ordering: The Royalty Asymmetry Calculator'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Seven-Eleven Japan AI ordering plus HQ-led markdown (Eco da Ne), Lawson AI.CO (ordering plus AI markdown recommendation), FamilyMart AI Recommend Ordering, Sinops (sinops-CLOUD AI markdown) with Sato. White space: No product found that is an independent owner-side payoff engine for Japanese convenience-store franchisees. Searches in Japanese and English returned no startup, SaaS or app that (a) uses the owner's actual royalty tier and disposal-share contract terms to compute order levels, (b) sets markdown timing from the owner's payoff, or (c) audits HQ AI recommendations against the owner's interest. HQ tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) cover order and markdown outputs but are HQ-controlled and aimed at waste or sales, not owner take-home. Supermarket AI-markdown vendors (Sinops/Sato, Wasteless) sell to retailers, not franchisees. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice with no calculators or automation. The unserved wedge is: HQ says X, your own contract math says Y, the yen difference is Z, plus contract-aware multi-store economics. Caveats: (1) Seven-Eleven's new contract (announced June 2026, effective autumn 2027) raises HQ's disposal-loss share from 15% to 50% (with a cap), lowers charge to 53%/67%, applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned for existing stores (https://www.ryutsuu.biz/strategy/s061915.html, https://www.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/news/2118977.html). At 50/50 the owner critical ratio rises from about 22% to roughly 36%, so the asymmetry mostly fades on new-contract stores but persists on legacy stores for years. (2) Seven's HQ-led markdown push since 2024 partly commoditizes the markdown clock. (3) The 22% vs 70% math checks out for the 85/15 split, but contract terms differ by chain (Lawson subsidy formula is more complex, FamilyMart is about 15%), so each chain needs its own model. (4) Franchise-agreement limits on data use and third-party tools were not verified. | How this version avoids them: It gives no ordering or markdown advice, so it does not compete with Seven, Lawson or FamilyMart AI, with Seven's markdown push, or with Sinops, Wasteless, Afresh and Shelf Engine, all of which are operational tools sold to retailers that inherit the retailer's payoff. Too Good To Go is an outlet for surplus. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice and community but no evidence base or data, so they become referral channels and cooperative allies. HQ tools are the subject being recorded, and they cannot copy an independent record of their own recommendations without undermining themselves. Power sources: network economies in the pooled index, a cornered resource in owner-contributed logs, switching costs in years of timestamped history.

title: Section 8 Rent-Increase Deadline Capture Service
one_liner: A tracker that knows each voucher tenant's lease anniversary, sees the new FY2027 payment standard, and files the landlord's rent-increase request inside the tight 60-day window before a year of raise is forfeited.
customer: Small landlords with 1 to 50 Housing Choice Voucher units, especially out-of-state investors in Section 8-heavy markets such as Memphis, Cleveland, St. Louis and Indianapolis. Small PM firms with voucher portfolios are the second segment.
problem: Housing-authority payment standards rose for FY2027, but a new standard does not flow through to an existing tenancy on October 1. It applies only at each tenant's lease anniversary. The owner must send a written request within a typically tight window, often 60 days before that date, or forfeit the increase for a year. Each housing authority has its own forms and dates. Most small owners never map the anniversary dates, so they leave real money uncollected. One market analysis found 3-bedroom increases of 6 to 12%, with a median of 10%.
solution: The landlord uploads photos of their HAP contracts and leases, and the tool extracts tenant anniversary dates and current contract rents. The team maintains a database of housing-authority payment standards and each authority's request process (scraped from PHA PDFs and notices, human-verified). For each unit it computes the increase headroom, alerts at 90, 75 and 60 days before the window closes, and generates the authority-specific rent-increase request letter or form. It tracks proof of submission and logs who was contacted and when. It also flags likely mistakes in the original rent-reasonableness record (wrong bedroom count or square footage) that justify a correction request mid-lease.
why_now: FY2027 standards take effect around October 1, 2026, and today is 2026-09-28. Anniversary windows are opening across the country right now. The forum thread on this appeared within days, and the one-year forfeiture is a hard deadline that makes people spend money.
revenue_model: Success-aligned pricing: $5 per unit per month, plus 1 month of the captured increase for each unit where the request is approved. On a $1,300 rent and a 10% bump, that is $130 per month, or $1,560 a year, per unit. Authority data is the moat; a PM-firm plan can charge per door. Later, a similar deadline tracker can cover annual recertification and inspection dates.
non_obvious_insight: The money is lost to a calendar, not to the tenant or the market, and the people who feel it are the least likely to be organized. A BiggerPockets post titled 'Section 8 rents went up for FY2027. Most landlords won't collect it' says: 'A new payment standard does not flow through to an existing tenancy on October 1'. It adds that owners must submit written requests within a typically tight 60-day window before each anniversary or forfeit the opportunity for an entire year. It reports 3-bedroom rates up 6-12% (median 10%) in nine of ten low-cost ZIP codes, and notes that St. Louis adopted its FY2027 standards effective Jan 1, 2027 (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/52/topics/1301792-section-8-rents-went-up-for-fy2027-most-landlords-wont-collect-it). Out-of-state voucher landlords also struggle with local rules, as in a Cleveland thread on Section 8 inspection standards (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302305-furnace-and-water-heater-on-wood-platforms-cleveland-section-8-inspection). A separate thread notes Section 8 tenants are 'already at maximum allowable rates' (https://www.biggerpockets.com/forums/963/topics/1302138-how-realistic-is-it-to-raise-rents-100-on-existing-tenants).
first_30_days: Week 1: hand-build payment-standard tables and request procedures for 3 housing authorities (start with St. Louis, Cleveland and Memphis). Publish a free calculator, 'How much did you leave on the table this year?', in the BiggerPockets Out-of-State and Landlording forums. Weeks 2 to 3: onboard 15 landlords, send requests manually with the templates, and track approvals. Week 4: turn on success-fee billing, and pitch 3 small voucher-heavy PM firms. Target: 15 landlords, 100+ units, and 10 documented approved increases.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: RentsPaid, HAPSecure, TenantKeep, VoucherReady. White space: The reminder and calendar layer is not open. RentsPaid, HAPSecure and TenantKeep already ship anniversary or rent-increase-window alerts at free to $39/mo, and TenantKeep advertises PHA letter generation. A plain tracker with alerts would be a fourth entrant selling against free. All of them are software-only and unfunded. What remains unserved is (1) actually filing the request and chasing it to approval, since TenantKeep says outright that it does not file; (2) a human-verified, authority-by-authority rulebook (window length, form, portal versus mail, comps requirement, tenant signature) in the Section 8-heavy investor markets: Memphis, Cleveland, St. Louis, Indianapolis; VoucherReady explicitly declines to supply PHA numbers; (3) contingency pricing tied to captured increase, when every competitor charges flat SaaS or free; (4) a portfolio leakage audit for small PM firms and out-of-state investors (units at or under the new payment standard with no filed request). Two caveats. Payment standard increases apply to the family's subsidy at the next regular reexam (24 CFR 982.505), not at the lease anniversary, so the pitch conflates two clocks. Rent reasonableness also caps the gain, and BiggerPockets commenters note many voucher units are already at the local maximum.

title: Contributor-Only Delay Outcome Ledger for Immigration Solos
one_liner: A give-to-get ledger that joins public dockets with the USCIS action dates only the filing lawyer sees, sold as a triage score plus a consent-order-first filing pack for a solo's existing stuck files in the four highest-moot districts.
customer: Solo and 2-5 attorney immigration firms whose book is mostly naturalization, family-based, I-751 and I-765 work, already admitted in E.D.N.Y., D.N.J., D. Conn. or E.D. Mich. (the districts where Mandamus.com's own tally shows 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action). Narrowest wedge: a firm holding 10+ files already past posted times or more than 120 days past a naturalization interview. Those are existing paying clients, so each filing is a $2.5-5k upsell with zero acquisition cost. Secondary buyers later: boutique mandamus firms and litigation funders, as data licensees.
problem: Solos sit on stuck files and do not file, for reasons the judges and the competitor research surfaced. (1) They cannot tell which suits will be quietly mooted and which will draw a motion to dismiss: nationality-hold suits went 0-13 in D.D.C. this summer, and the Fifth Circuit bars I-485 delay claims (Cheejati). (2) They cannot price a flat fee without knowing the tail if the government fights. (3) A free pro se guide plus a $5,000 boutique make a $400 drafting tool look redundant, and general AI drafting is eroding the 6-10 hour learning curve. Public stats are hand-tallied for about 7 districts, and a docket shows when a case ended, not why or when USCIS actually acted.
solution: Three pieces, all attorney-of-record signed (the company is software). (1) Stuck-Case Book: paste or CSV-import pending cases from any case-management export (no partnership needed). It ranks each file by ripeness and expected days from service to USCIS action. Ripeness is tiered: N-400s more than 120 days after interview under 8 U.S.C. 1447(b), where the statute supplies the clock and in most circuits USCIS cannot adjudicate until the court remands, come first; then I-751, I-765 and long-idle I-130/I-140 under the APA. It refuses to generate filings for nationality-hold and Fifth Circuit I-485 cases and says why. (2) Filing pack: complaint, exhibits, service checklist, 60-day answer calendar, a documented pre-suit exhaustion checklist (e-request, Ombudsman, congressional inquiry) that also builds the 'not substantially justified' record, and a consent-order-first settlement template with an express EAJA reservation and a 30-day fee-petition reminder. (3) The ledger: after each case the attorney logs service date, USCIS action date and how it ended (consent order, quiet adjudication, MTD granted or denied). Judge- and AUSA-level detail unlocks only for contributors; everyone else gets a free coarse district scorecard.
why_now: The Oct 2025 end of the 540-day EAD auto-extension made I-765 delay suits a primary remedy, and holds keep files idle, but D.D.C.'s June-Aug 2026 record (government 13-0) means undifferentiated 'just file' now loses, so triage suddenly has value it lacked two years ago. LLM drafting has turned complaint templates into a commodity, pushing value to judgment and data. Honest caveat: RECAP counts look flat (385, 352, 477 filings a year in 2023-25), so the pitch is a higher win rate per filing, not a volume surge.
revenue_model: Free: coarse district scorecard (lead magnet and SEO). Paid: $299/month Ledger Pro (unlimited Stuck-Case Book, 2 filing packs a month, judge/AUSA-level data for contributors), extra packs $250 each. Flat fees only, never a share of the lawyer's fee. Year 2: data licenses ($1-3k/month) to boutique firms, litigation funders and case-management vendors. Bottom-up (assumptions to validate): about 1,500 target solos in the four districts x 20% penetration x about $3.6k/year is roughly $1.1M ARR before adding districts.
non_obvious_insight: A docket records when a suit ended, not when or why USCIS acted; stipulations and the 60-day answer clock add weeks of noise. The real key is service date, then USCIS action date, then dismissal type, and only the filing lawyer holds the approval notice. Every competing stat (Mandamus.com's hand tally, Lex Machina/Trellis-style docket analytics, raw CourtListener) is blind to it, so the moat is a cornered resource that accrues only through contributors and cannot be scraped. Second, the solo's blocking question is not 'can I draft this' but 'what does it cost me if the government fights'; tail probability by district is what lets them quote a confident flat fee.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: run the 8 real web searches the prior research could not (mandamus AI, delay-suit software, Crunchbase, AILA toolkits). Days 1-21: hand-label roughly 300 USCIS delay dockets from 2023-26 in E.D.N.Y., D.N.J., D. Conn. and E.D. Mich. from CourtListener/RECAP (cause of ending, days to end) and publish a free district scorecard. Days 7-30: pull the roughly 60 attorneys of record who file most of those suits (public) and offer free lifetime Founding Contributor status in exchange for backfilling 10 past cases with USCIS action dates from their approval notices; separately offer 100+ non-filing solos in the same districts a free 10-minute Stuck-Case Book audit of their own pending files and pre-sell 5 at $299/month. Go/no-go: 5 paying firms and 100+ outcomes with action dates logged by day 30.
lineage: mutation of I1062 ('Delay-Suit Rails for Stuck Immigration Cases'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Bertollini / Mandamus.com (immigration mandamus boutique), Docketwise (immigration case-management software), Alma (tryalma.com, immigration law firm plus tech), Boundless (consumer immigration services). White space: Important caveat first. The WebSearch budget was already spent (200 of 200) before I started, so I ran no web searches at all. I used direct fetches of guessed or known URLs, CourtListener's API and GitHub search. This means 'no direct software competitor found' is weaker evidence than normal. One attempt to load a Google results page returned nothing and was not used. Before committing, someone should run 6-8 real searches (for example 'mandamus AI immigration', 'delay lawsuit software immigration attorneys', Crunchbase, YC, and the AILA and AIC toolkits).

What I found: no software or platform that sells attorney-signed, white-label mandamus filing plus a per-district rules library plus outcome analytics to solo immigration lawyers. The only direct-service players are boutique law firms selling the suit to end clients. Mandamus.com does this at $5,000 plus $500 and gives away templates, and the practice-management incumbent Docketwise has no such feature. The open data (CourtListener) and free guides make the raw ingredients cheap for anyone.

The genuinely unserved wedge is narrow. It is a pre-filing 'will this get mooted or dismissed here' triage, based on real district-by-form-type outcome data, plus a ready-to-file pack for routine delays in the districts where the government usually adjudicates rather than litigates (per Mandamus.com's own data: EDNY, D. Conn., DNJ and EDMI at 83-85% voluntary dismissal after agency action).

Parts of the pitch look weak against what I found:
(1) Nationality-hold suits look poor. Per Mandamus.com's summary of 13 D.D.C. delay decisions from June to August 2026, the government won all 13. Judge Leon in the consolidated Ivanov case found the categorical pause unexplained but dismissed the delay and mandamus counts under TRAC and limited relief to named plaintiffs. A 'nationality hold' template is a liability, not a hook.
(2) S.D. Tex., one of the five launch districts, is hostile. Cheejati v. Blinken (5th Cir. 2024) bars I-485 delay claims on jurisdictional grounds, and DOJ there files motions to dismiss rather than negotiate.
(3) Buckhannon: when USCIS simply adjudicates, the plaintiff is not a prevailing party and can't recover EAJA fees (typically $4,000-$12,000 only if a consent order is obtained). The flat fee holds up, but the 'forced deadline' product should be structured around consent orders.
(4) The '6-10 hour learning curve' is being eroded by free content and general AI drafting.
(5) The data moat is thin. CourtListener docket data is free, and the boutique firms already publish their own district stats. | How this version avoids them: Mandamus.com sells suits to consumers at $5,000 and has no lawyer-facing product; this targets its would-be referrers, treats it as a data buyer, and builds a joined dataset it cannot hand-tally. Docketwise has no litigation features; this rides on CSV export so it does not depend on it, and if Docketwise adds templates it still cannot copy a contributor-fed ledger. Lex Machina/Trellis and CourtListener see docket events only, not agency action dates or consent-versus-quiet outcomes; this builds on CourtListener rather than competing with it. DoNotPay and general AI drafting compete on drafting; this sells calibrated judgment (which suit, where, with what settlement structure) and refuses bad cases. Alma and Boundless are consumer or visa firms, not tools, and are potential customers.

title: IEP Chief of Staff for Special-Ed Parents
one_liner: Rich parents win school disputes with a paid educational advocate and paper trail; for $20/mo, give parents of the roughly 7.5M US students with IEPs a chief of staff who watches the legal clocks and logs every missed service minute.
customer: Parents of children with IEPs (autism, ADHD, dyslexia, speech and language delay), sold through state and local special-ed parent groups, parent training centers, pediatric practices, disability law clinics and credit unions.
problem: Districts arrive with a team; wealthy families bring an advocate ($150-400/hr) and an attorney. Federal enforcement was hollowed out (mass OSEP layoffs in October 2025, and reported moves of oversight to HHS and civil-rights enforcement to DOJ in June 2026), so parents are effectively on their own. Most violations are procedural (late evaluations, missing prior written notice, services not delivered) and go unnoticed because nobody keeps the clocks.
solution: Parent uploads the IEP and evaluations. The system builds the legal calendar (evaluation timelines from consent, meeting-notice windows, annual and triennial reviews, progress-report cadence), drafts records requests, creates a one-page pre-meeting brief (top asks plus data), and sends a same-day 'memorializing' follow-up email with prior-written-notice requests after meetings. It logs service minutes delivered vs promised, quantifying missed minutes for a compensatory-services claim, and scans the IEP for defects (no baselines, unmeasurable goals). Advocates are on-demand at $75 per 30 minutes, with a path to state complaint and due process.
why_now: The federal special-ed enforcement vacuum is documented and new as of late 2025 and mid-2026. IEP counts are rising, and LLMs can parse messy IEP PDFs and draft procedurally precise letters. Parent communities are organized on Facebook and Reddit and actively looking for help.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family; $75 advocate sessions with a revenue split to a vetted advocate co-op; $3-6 per member per month from parent centers, pediatric groups and credit unions; district-facing analytics sold only with parent consent, later.
non_obvious_insight: What the rich buy is not better argument but continuous procedural pressure: dated, written, specific requests. The subscription funds clock-watching and documentation, not advice. Parents who log service minutes turn 'I feel they're not delivering' into a quantified claim, and the paper trail is the evidence in any later dispute, so value compounds over time.
first_30_days: Publish a free IEP clock calculator and letter templates. Partner with admins of 10 state-level special-ed Facebook groups and concierge 30 families manually, measuring violations found. Convert those families to $20/mo and recruit 5 advocates for the on-demand tier.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: IEP Advocate.ai, ChatGPT and general LLMs (endorsed by CADRE's parent guide), Parent Training and Information Centers (PTIs/CPRCs), Wrightslaw. White space: Confidence is moderate-low. The WebSearch budget hit 200/200 before I could run the planned 6-12 searches, so I found competitors mostly by fetching guessed and known URLs. More direct competitors probably exist that I did not see, and this should be re-run once the search limit is raised.

The core pitch is NOT white space. Deadline extraction, procedural letter generation, meeting prep briefs and state-complaint drafting are already live at IEP Advocate.ai for $30/mo. Free ChatGPT covers much of the rest. A $20/mo 'AI IEP chief of staff' would be a cheaper copy.

Specific gaps I could not find served in the pages I reached:
1. A service-delivery ledger. This means logging minutes promised vs delivered per IEP service line and turning the shortfall into a compensatory-services claim packet. IEP Advocate.ai's fetched pages do not describe service-minute logging or comp-ed calculation.
2. Human-in-the-loop verification. CADRE and K-12 Dive document AI-drafted complaints with fabricated case law and wrong IDEA readings. A product that combines grounded output with vetted advocate or attorney review, at $75 per 30 minutes, is unserved. IEP Advocate.ai has no human tier.
3. B2B2C distribution through parent centers, disability law clinics, pediatric practices and credit unions at $3-6 per member per month. IEP Advocate.ai lists only individual pricing. The channel is unproven.
4. Evidence-grade record keeping. Time-stamped, tamper-evident logs that a hearing officer will accept, rather than chat history.

title: Rural County Night Desk for Hospitals and Jails
one_liner: One pool of licensed remote night nurses and NPs sold as a county bundle: the recorded independent second RN for the critical access hospital, and the video screening that lets a deputy clear an arrestee for booking without a four-hour ER trip.
customer: Chief nursing officers and pharmacy directors at critical access hospitals, county sheriffs and commissioners, state hospital associations, county risk pools, and malpractice and captive insurers, all reached through the same rural-county channels.
problem: At 3am a rural county has three nurses on at the hospital and one or two deputies on the road. The nurse who is supposed to witness a narcotic waste or double-check a high-alert drug is mid-code, and the deputy with an arrestee is stuck in that same ER for hours, leaving the county unpatrolled. Each problem alone is too small to support a dedicated clinical team.
solution: Start with the $150 tablet-and-camera cart at the dispensing cabinet: a remote RN appears within 60 seconds, watches the waste on video, and attests, with a time-stamped clip and an audit log matched to the cabinet record. Add a booking-desk kit (vitals, pulse oximeter, glucometer, breathalyzer) with a physician-signed, ACEP-based clearance protocol and 24/7 RN and NP video screening ('fit for booking with monitoring plan', 'needs ER now', 're-check in 2 hours'). Both run on one recording platform, one compact-licensed clinician pool, one supervising physician and one malpractice policy. The county gets a single dashboard showing diversion-audit coverage, ER visits avoided and 'deputy hours returned to patrol'.
why_now: Rural hospitals are staffed thinly at night and rural jail deaths and diversion are in the news, so both insurers and risk pools are actively looking for evidence-grade controls. Compact licensure and cheap video hardware let a small team run a multi-state night pool for the first time.
revenue_model: $1,500-2,500 per hospital per month plus per-event fees above volume, and $2,000-3,500 per county per month for about 40 jail screens plus $85 per extra screen, so roughly $4-6k per month for a county bundle. Discounts through malpractice insurers and county risk pools convert to distribution. Gross margin of 40-50% at a pool of about 8-12 hospitals per RN per night.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is the same: a credentialed, recorded, independent clinician on camera at 3am, with a defensible protocol. The evidence infrastructure (timestamped video, audit log, physician-signed protocol) that proves a diversion witness also proves a jail clearance, so one product convinces both insurers. Waste events cluster around medication passes while booking clusters around bar close and weekends, so the two workloads plausibly smooth each other out, and a pilot can confirm that before hiring. The hospital is a natural co-payer, since every cleared arrestee is an ER visit it no longer has to staff for free.
first_30_days: The founder, a rural ER nurse, recruits 6 per-diem or retired RNs with compact licenses plus 1-2 NPs on remote night hours. Write the clearance protocol with a supervising rural-ER physician and have one county attorney review it. Pick one county with both a critical access hospital and a jail the founder knows. Offer the hospital a free 30-day cabinet pilot and the sheriff a $1,500, 60-day booking-desk pilot. Bring the combined numbers (waste attestations logged, ER trips avoided, deputy hours saved) to the state hospital association and the county risk pool.
lineage: hybrid of I0016 + I1025 (Remote Second-RN for Rural Night Shifts + Tele-Clearance for Sheriffs' Booking Desks). Why stronger: Each parent has the same expensive fixed costs (clinician recruiting, compact licenses, recording platform, physician oversight, malpractice) and a small revenue per site. Pooling spreads those costs over two products sold to overlapping counties, lets one relationship close a larger $4-6k per month deal, and lets two insurers see one shared evidence trail, which raises ACV and lowers cost per sale versus either service alone.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: MIDAS Healthcare Solutions (MidasVIEW / Anytime Witness, aka V.I.E.W.), BD Pyxis Med Link Queue & Waste, Avel eCare, VirtuAlly (with Teledigm Health). White space: Nobody I found sells a shared, pooled, live remote-RN witness subscription to critical access hospitals. The specific gaps are:
(1) Live human supply. MidasVIEW replaces the second person with recorded video reviewed later. Pyxis remote witness still needs a colleague on shift. Virtual-nursing vendors cover admissions, discharges, sitters and documentation. Remote pharmacy vendors cover order verification. Nobody provides a licensed second person on demand at 3am.
(2) Transfusion, high-alert and pediatric double-checks. Asynchronous video cannot substitute for a live independent check before administration. Remote IDC is documented as feasible but under-evidenced, and only a few institutions do it (ONS 2024).
(3) Small-hospital fit. MidasVIEW pilots are at tertiary and children's hospitals. Small facilities lag on diversion controls: only 57% of single facilities actively monitor camera footage, and CAHs lack pharmacy staff to review video the next day.
(4) Insurer-linked audit trail. No diversion vendor sells to liability or captive insurers.
The wedge is narrow and time-limited. Avel eCare, VirtuAlly and the telepharmacy vendors could add a witness line quickly, and MidasVIEW could add live witness routing. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: NaphCare (STATCare 24/7 telehealth), Wellpath, Southern Health Partners, Turn Key Health. White space: Caveat first: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I could run any searches, so this verdict rests on about 14 direct page fetches. That is far short of the 6-12 searches the task called for, and I found no startup-specific evidence either way. I found no vendor whose page shows a tele-clearance product for booking desks, meaning a remote RN/NP screening arrestees before booking with a time-stamped disposition (fit for booking, needs ER now, re-check in 2 hours). Incumbent jail-health vendors (Wellpath, NaphCare, Southern Health Partners) sell on-site staffing or in-custody care. Avel eCare sells 24/7 virtual clinicians to rural ERs and to law enforcement, but only for behavioral crisis. The unserved wedge is a pre-booking, per-county-per-month subscription for jails too small to justify a contracted health vendor, priced against deputy-hours and ER bills. Hospital-run or jail-staff-run tele-clearance programs may already exist locally and I could not check.\n\nTwo structural risks weaken the wedge and need validating early. First, the pitch says the Nurse Licensure Compact makes cross-state night staffing workable, but the NLC covers RNs, not NPs. As far as I know the APRN Compact was not yet operational, so NP staffing likely needs per-state licenses. Second, a remote clinician clearing an intoxicated or injured person on vitals and video alone shifts head-injury and withdrawal liability onto the vendor. That is a malpractice-insurance and clinical-governance problem, and a risk pool may or may not accept it. Revenue is also thin: 12 counties at $2-3.5k a month is roughly $290k-500k a year, with slow county sales cycles.

title: Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers
one_liner: A phone-based monthly proof-of-work ledger that turns gig, cash and self-employment activity into state-accepted documentation and 30-day cure packets, paid for by the Medicaid plans and health centers that lose revenue when members drop.
customer: Medicaid managed care organizations with expansion-adult lines, and FQHC and community health center networks. Medicaid is 43-50% of health center revenue, and an MCO is paid capitation per member-month. End users are expansion adults aged 19-64 with irregular income. The MCO or health center pays per retained member; the enrollee pays nothing.
problem: CMS's interim final rule (June 3, 2026) requires states to implement 80 hours a month of work or activity, or $580 a month in income, by Jan 1, 2027. Compliance is checked at application and at renewal, and a noncompliance notice gives 30 calendar days to cure. CBO projects about 4.8M coverage losses from work requirements, largely from reporting complexity. About 9 in 10 affected patients are expected to qualify for an exemption or already comply, yet many will still lose coverage on documentation. Nebraska went live May 1, 2026 with self-attestation, but about 28,000 people there must document twice a year and the state plans to move to verification.
solution: An enrollee-side SMS and app tool. It ingests bank and payment-app statements, gig platform earnings exports (Uber, DoorDash, Cash App, Venmo), pay stub photos and logged volunteer or class hours. It computes whether each month clears $580 or 80 hours and generates the state-specific verification packet. It sends look-back-month reminders and prepares the 30-day cure response. It flags likely exemption candidates, such as medically frail members, from plan claims data. The plan or clinic dashboard shows at-risk members and cure success. The tool only assists and never determines compliance, which is what federal rules allow plans to do.
why_now: The interim final rule was published June 3, 2026, and the national start date is Jan 1, 2027. Nebraska's live rollout is the preview of what other states will face when verification replaces self-attestation. CMS is encouraging automation, but states are spending on caseworker portals, notices and screening tools, not on income documentation for gig workers.
revenue_model: $3-8 per at-risk member per month billed to the MCO, or a success fee of $50-150 per member retained through renewal. FQHC SaaS at $2-5k per month per site with an outcomes dashboard. Later, state contracts for a self-employed and gig documentation module.
non_obvious_insight: Vendors such as Salesforce are building state-facing portals for applicants and caseworkers. The parties with a P&L at stake, the MCOs and health centers, are not yet being sold a member-side tool. KFF's roundup of state outreach plans covers notices, websites and screening tools but does not describe how self-employed or irregular income will be documented (https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-work-requirements-federal-outreach-requirements-and-state-plans/). State wage-data matching misses 1099, cash and gig work by design. Georgetown's CCF warns that 'verification in this context means burdensome documentation requirements for enrollees' (https://ccf.georgetown.edu/2026/05/11/the-new-medicaid-work-reporting-requirements-are-here-dont-let-the-nebraska-soft-start-fool-you/). The retention math is lopsided: a plan or clinic can pay a few dollars a month per member to protect several hundred dollars of monthly revenue. Sources: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/06/03/2026-11094/medicaid-program-community-engagement-requirement-for-certain-individuals and https://www.pointcare.com/blog/how-to-prevent-medicaid-coverage-gaps-in-2026
first_30_days: Build the Nebraska flow first, since it is already live. Recruit 50 gig and self-employed Medicaid enrollees through one FQHC partner. Measure how many can produce a compliant $580 or 80-hour packet within 30 days. Take those results to two MCO member-engagement and quality leads for a paid pilot. Sign an LOI with one health center network before Jan 1, 2027.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CMS Emmy (Eligibility Made Easy) app and Emmy API, SteadyIQ (Income Passport / Verification Hub), Digital Public Works, Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam/Merative (state-side community engagement modules). White space: Nobody I found sells an enrollee-side monthly ledger to MCOs or FQHCs that ingests bank, gig and pay-stub data, computes $580 or 80 hours against a state's look-back rules, and produces a state-specific 30-day cure packet. Nothing turned up in searches, CMS vendor pledges or CBPP/KFF/Georgetown landscape coverage. Vendors sit on either side of that gap. State-side vendors (SteadyIQ, Emmy, Maximus, Optum, Deloitte) sell to state agencies. Provider and plan-side vendors (Pointcare, Findhelp, mPulse) sell eligibility monitoring and outreach without gig-income packet building. The clearest unserved segment is workers with no digital trail: cash, informal and 1099-below-threshold workers such as day labor, cleaning and landscaping. Consent-based verification (CBV) via payroll, bank or gig platforms cannot reach them. The 30-day cure step, meaning a compiled packet after a noncompliance notice, is also not addressed by any product I found. The wedge is narrow and could close quickly. States with CBV (SteadyIQ, Emmy) let the enrollee connect accounts directly, which makes a separate packet redundant there. MCOs may be poor buyers because the IFR bars plans from determining compliance and gives them only a supporting role. Pointcare and Findhelp already own the FQHC and MCO relationships and could add a module. Research limits: my web search budget ran out after four searches, so I relied on page fetches. I could not load the CBPP vendor landscape, the Health Affairs piece or the Federal Register text (all blocked), and I could not confirm what Propel for Plans does or any vendor's funding.

title: Unwind Desk for California's 3-Day Car Return
one_liner: A per-return concierge that unwinds a cancelled used-car deal (lender, add-on administrators, DMV, sales tax, commissions) inside California's new 48-hour refund deadline. It then turns the return data into a return-risk pool.
customer: California used-car dealers, especially independents and BHPH lots that sell 30 to 200 used cars a month and have no back-office bench. They pay $195 to $250 per return, or a standby retainer. Later, insurers and MGAs buy the underwriting data.
problem: From Oct 1, 2026, SB 766 gives buyers a 3-day right to cancel a used vehicle priced at $50,000 or less. Within 48 hours of cancellation the dealer must cancel the contract and refund the buyer, less only the deductions the law allows for mileage and damage. That is easy to write and very hard to do. The cost of an unwind is the cascade, not the car. The dealer has to reach the lender that has funded or is holding the contract, cancel each service contract and GAP with its administrator, and charge back the F&I commission. It also has to reverse the title, registration and sales tax, refund the down payment and any trade, and document the vehicle condition to justify any deduction. Independents have never done this at volume, and one botched unwind creates a refund violation and a private-plaintiff claim.
solution: Unwind-as-a-service. The dealer forwards the cancellation notice. The desk runs a checklist workflow that notifies the lender, submits cancellations to administrators with the correct pro-rata or full-refund basis, prepares the DMV and tax reversals, calculates the refund and permitted deductions, and produces a compliance file that meets the two-year retention rule. A delivery-day photo and video capture link is bundled, because permitted deductions depend on condition documentation. After 6 months of volume, the desk holds the only dataset on return rates, timing and loss per return in a mandatory-return regime. That data is enough to price a per-unit return-risk cover (roughly $60 to $120 per used unit) through a licensed MGA or insurer partner.
why_now: The law takes effect Oct 1, 2026, so the first returns arrive within days. No US state has had a mandatory 3-day return on used cars at this scale. The 2025 to 2026 run of subprime stress, roughly 30% of trade-ins underwater and repossessions at about 3M a year, means many buyers will discover mid-week that they can't afford the payment. That is the buyer most likely to use the cancellation right.
revenue_model: Flat fee per processed return ($195 to $250). Standby retainer of about $99 per month per store for priority handling. Phase 2: 10 to 20% of premium as an MGA on the return-risk pool. Phase 3: license the cancellation-cascade workflow to DMS and eContract vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody knows the real return rate. Everyone models it on Carvana's 7-day return, but the buyers who return are not typical, because the F&I office sees payment shock and buyer's remorse first. A 48-hour refund deadline is shorter than the time a lender, administrator or DMV normally takes to process anything, so the dealer's exposure is process failure, not vehicle depreciation. Whoever owns the process owns the data, and the data is what makes the insurance product priceable.
first_30_days: Write the cascade checklist by state and by lender for the 20 most common California indirect lenders and 15 administrators. Approach the California Independent Automobile Dealers Association and 10 high-volume independents. Sell a $99 per month standby plan with a guaranteed 24-hour turnaround per return. Handle the first 20 returns manually with a shared spreadsheet and e-sign before writing any software. Log every step's time and dollar cost, since that log becomes the actuarial dataset.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ComplyAuto (exclusively licensed by CNCDA), CDK Global (DMS), CNCDA (California New Car Dealers Association), DealerCenter (DMS for independent dealers). White space: Research limitation: the WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200), so no searches were run. That means no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches, and no search for startups by name. Everything below comes from direct WebFetch of about 30 primary and vendor URLs, with model-generated page summaries. I found NO dedicated 'unwind-as-a-service' for CARS Act cancellations, but I cannot rule out a small startup. Re-run the startup and forum searches before committing.

The idea's premise is weaker than written. Statute text (SB 766, Civ. Code 1784.43, 1784.31(g), 1784.44, as returned by WebFetch and quoted verbatim by the summarizer):
1. The 48-hour duty is only to cancel the contract and refund the buyer. The dealer 'is not responsible for any delays outside the control of the dealer, including delays attributable to the processing of a refund by a bank, credit card company, or other financial institution.' Check payments get a 2-business-day delay. Lender and administrator lag therefore does not create violation exposure. The exposure is the dealer's cash float and its own process failures.
2. The statute lists no duty to cancel service contracts or GAP within 48 hours. The add-on cascade is a business and recovery problem, governed by existing law and contract terms. It is not a statutory deadline.
3. Permitted deductions are formulaic: a restocking fee of 1.5% of price (min $200, max $600), plus $1 per mile over 250 (capped at $150), plus trade-in liens. They are not damage-based. The claim that permitted deductions depend on condition documentation, which justifies the photo and video capture bundle, does not hold up. What does matter is the 400-mile eligibility gate and the trade-in refund rule. If the trade-in is already sold or in title transfer, the refund is the greater of the agreed value, the sale price, or fair market value.
4. Remedies are non-exclusive (1784.22). No explicit private right of action or civil penalty was found. Enforcement runs through DAs, city attorneys and the DMV, plus existing consumer laws.
5. Dealers already run unwinds. California had a 2-day contract cancellation option with a 2-day refund including sales tax (Veh. Code 11713.21), repealed effective Oct 1, 2026. Failed-financing spot-delivery unwinds are also routine (from my background knowledge, not verified here). Buy-here-pay-here lots hold their own paper, so they have no lender cascade at all. The $195 to $250 per-return price competes with a title clerk or F&I manager plus a DMS 'reverse deal' function.

What remains unserved:
(a) Independent, indirect-financed dealers with no back-office bench. Compliance vendors and associations found are aimed at franchised dealers or at pricing, ad and disclosure compliance.
(b) A per-return calculator and checklist: restocking fee, mileage, the trade-in 'greater of three' refund, lender payoff, F&I commission chargeback, and the administrator-by-administrator cancellation basis, with timers and a 2-year compliance file.
(c) Above all, the dealer's economic loss per return. Dealers lost the fee they could charge for the old cancellation option ($75 to $250 or 1%). Restocking is now capped at $200 to $600, against recon, carrying cost and resale loss. Nobody was found pricing or covering that loss.

title: Orphan Lien Clearance Desk for Title Agents
one_liner: A flat-fee curative service that proves dead solar fixture filings and other zombie liens are dead (or gets them released) so home closings stop stalling.
customer: Independent title and escrow agencies and real estate attorneys in high-solar states (AZ, CA, FL, TX, NJ, NC, NV, CO), billed per file and usually paid by the seller at closing. Listing agents in solar-heavy markets are a second channel.
problem: Sunnova filed Chapter 11 in June 2025 (500,000+ customers), Mosaic and PosiGen followed, and the residential solar credit ended for 2026 installs, so thousands of homes carry UCC-1 fixture filings and recorded solar-lease notices held by dead, merged or reassigned entities. Title examiners flag every one. Agents can't tell who holds the debt now, whether the filing is even still legally effective, or how to get a termination, so closings slip days or weeks. The people currently serving this are consumer SEO and lead-gen sites, not the title agents who actually need it solved on a deadline.
solution: Per-file lien autopsy delivered in 48 hours. (1) Pull the recorded instrument and any continuation or termination filings from the county index and the Secretary of State. (2) Compute lapse under UCC 9-515 (five years unless continued in the six-month window). (3) Trace the assignment and servicer chain through bankruptcy dockets and servicer notices. (4) Deliver either an underwriter-ready 'lapsed, no exception' memo, or a payoff/estoppel request plus a pre-drafted termination (UCC-3, or debtor-filed termination where the statute allows) recorded in that county's required format. Recorded memoranda of lease, which do not lapse, get a release workflow instead. Later expand the same engine to satisfied-but-never-released mortgages, expired judgment liens, dead PACE liens and resurfaced zombie second mortgages.
why_now: 2025-2026 solar installer bankruptcies (Sunnova, Mosaic, PosiGen) and the end of the residential solar credit produced the largest single wave of orphaned fixture filings ever recorded. 2018-2021 installs are now hitting their five-year lapse dates just as those homes come to market. Title agents are short-staffed and want to outsource curative work, and an LLM can read county index entries and bankruptcy docket text cheaply.
revenue_model: Flat fee of about $395-$900 per cleared file, contingent on clear-to-close. Agencies with volume pay $299/month plus a reduced per-file rate. White-label API for underwriters and closing software later.
non_obvious_insight: Half the 'problem liens' in solar-heavy counties are already legally dead, but the county index never shows lapse, so examiners treat a 2019 fixture filing as live forever. Clerks watch continuation filings come in, and most small installers never filed one. The work is proof of death, not payoff. Insiders also know the recorded 'notice of lease' is a different animal that never lapses, and that a clerk must record a debtor-filed termination on its face, since the office is ministerial.
first_30_days: Offer the first five files free to 3-5 independent title agencies in Phoenix, Tampa and Sacramento. Build the lapse calculator and county-index lookups for about 10 counties. Get one regional agent underwriter to accept a standard lapse-memo format. Then price at $495 per file and ask each agency for a testimonial and two referrals to listing agents.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SunStrong Management (successor servicer for the Sunnova book), Wolters Kluwer Lien Solutions / CSC (UCC search, filing, continuation and termination vendors), Qualia (title/escrow closing platform), Nationwide Title Clearing / national title-clearing and lien-release outsourcers (ServiceLink, etc.). White space: Research limits: the session's WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted, so I ran no searches. I used direct fetches of known URLs (Wikipedia, Cornell LII for the UCC text, SunStrong, Sunnova, Qualia, TitleCapture, Simplifile, the YC directory) and a GitHub repo search. Several guessed URLs 404'd or returned 403. Competitor coverage is therefore thin, and I found no funded startup doing solar-specific lien-lapse analysis and curative for title agents. Absence in my results is weak evidence, not proof.

Unserved as far as I could tell: a title-agent-facing, per-file workflow that (a) classifies the instrument (UCC-1 fixture filing vs. SOS-only filing vs. recorded memorandum or notice of lease vs. PACE vs. mortgage), (b) computes lapse under UCC 9-515, and (c) routes the file to the current servicer with a pre-formatted payoff, estoppel or UCC-3 request. Incumbent UCC vendors and general title-clearing outsourcers do not appear to package this for solar.

Substantive weaknesses to weigh against the gap:
- Lapse is not death. Cornell LII (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-515) confirms that on lapse the interest becomes unperfected, and is deemed never perfected only as against a purchaser for value. The debt and the interest against the debtor survive. In a lease or PPA the lessor owns the equipment, so a lapse memo does not clear ownership or the lease. The buyer still needs an assumption or buyout. Underwriters may therefore refuse to rely on 'lapsed, no exception' memos, and getting one to accept a format is the make-or-break step.
- Debtor-filed terminations are narrow. UCC 9-509(d)(2) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/9/9-509) requires the secured party to have failed to comply with 9-513, plus debtor authorization and a statement on the form. That generally means a demand and a wait, and it only works where no obligation is still secured. That conflicts with a 48-hour SLA.
- The 'orphan' premise is overstated for Sunnova, the biggest name. Its assets went to new owners and SunStrong runs a home-sale transfer process. The truly orphaned pool (Mosaic, PosiGen, small defunct installers) is smaller and messier. Sunnova is confirmed only via Wikipedia and the SunStrong and Sunnova sites. I could not fetch a Mosaic or PosiGen page.
- Unauthorized-practice-of-law exposure for underwriter-facing lapse opinions unless an attorney of record signs.
- Per-county recording quirks make it operations-heavy, not pure software.

title: Continuity Retainer for One-Licensee Funeral Homes
one_liner: Key-person insurance for funeral homes: a bench of pre-credentialed licensed directors and embalmers who step in within 24-48 hours when the owner is sick, burned out or gone, with a built-in path to succession.
customer: Independent and rural funeral homes with one or two licensed staff (roughly 30-150 calls a year), typically owner-operators aged 55-75. A second buyer is the family of an owner who has died or fallen ill and needs the home kept legal while it is sold.
problem: States require a licensed funeral director or manager-in-charge, and often a licensed embalmer, for an establishment to operate. The owner is on call 24/7/365 and hasn't had a real week off in years. One heart attack, surgery or burnout means the home cannot legally operate, families get funneled to the consolidator down the road, and a business built over three generations is sold at a distressed price. Informal 'relief director' phone lists exist, but there is no bench, no contract, no reciprocity or board paperwork handled, and no guarantee anyone answers at 3 a.m.
solution: Recruit retired and semi-retired licensed directors and embalmers, including many leaving consolidators, and pre-credential them in a target state cluster with background checks and reciprocity filings. Sell continuity retainers that guarantee a set number of coverage days a year (real vacations, weekends off) plus emergency activation within 24-48 hours at a day rate. The company handles the state-board notice of interim manager changes. A succession track lets an interim operator or next-generation licensed buyer convert into a partner or buyer with seller financing, so owners have an alternative to a roll-up.
why_now: Consolidation keeps shrinking the independent pool (SCI alone bought about 22 funeral homes and 2 cemeteries for roughly $101M in 2025). The licensed workforce is aging while mortuary-school pipelines are thin. Rising cremation lowers revenue per case, making full-time second hires unaffordable for small homes. Rural closures are creating 'funeral deserts'. Many states have passed occupational-license recognition laws that make multi-state relief staffing easier.
revenue_model: Retainer of $900-$2,000/month per home including N coverage days. Activation day rate of $800-$1,400 billed to the home, with a 25-30% margin over what the licensee is paid. Per-case fees for trade embalming and prep-room services. A 1-2% success fee on succession transactions.
non_obvious_insight: The real asset of an independent funeral home isn't the building, it's one license holder with a phone, and that is a single point of failure. Consolidators know it and wait. Owners will pay to sleep: this is a wellness and continuity product disguised as staffing, and its best feature is the succession pipeline it creates once a trusted operator is already inside the home.
first_30_days: Recruit eight retired licensed directors and embalmers through state association chapters and retiree groups. Check each state board's rules for temporary manager-in-charge designation. Pitch 20 one-licensee homes in two adjacent counties at a $1,200/month founding rate with a 'test weekend off' guarantee. Sign the first three, and run the first covered weekend within 30 days to produce a testimonial.
