Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: NFDA Funeral Career Hub and NFDA recruiting services, NFDA succession planning member resources and SESCO HR consulting, Selected Independent Funeral Homes (staff recruitment and Selected Transfer Services), American Mortuary Service (trade embalming and removals, Dallas/Fort Worth). White space: Caveat first: this verdict has low-to-moderate confidence. The WebSearch budget for the session was already exhausted (200 of 200), so none of the planned 6-12 searches ran. I did not use WebFetch on a search engine to get around the limit. All I did was fetch about 15 specific vendor and industry URLs. Most guessed domains did not resolve, and the ones that resolved were adjacent players, not direct competitors. "No direct competitor found" therefore means "not found with a very limited method", not "verified absent".

What the limited evidence supports as unserved: (1) A contracted, pre-credentialed, multi-state bench with a guaranteed activation SLA. The only related products I could confirm are a job board (NFDA), an association recruiting and transfer program (Selected), trade embalming vendors (American Mortuary Service) and member-only succession content (NFDA). None of them takes on the license-holder single point of failure. (2) The bundled path from interim operator to succession buyer with seller financing. I found nobody offering it, and it is the strongest differentiator because it turns a cost centre into a deal pipeline.

Risks I could not verify and that could still kill or reshape the idea, all of which come from the idea file and general reasoning, not from research:
- State law. Many boards tie the establishment license to a named manager-in-charge who must be there full-time or on premises, and some have short or no temporary-designation windows. If temporary designation is unavailable in the target states, the 24-48 hour activation promise fails legally. Check this first, state by state.
- Adverse selection and price. $10.8k-24k a year is roughly 2-8% of revenue for a home doing 30-150 calls, and a retainer is bought mostly by owners who feel at risk.
- Liability, insurance and non-solicit exposure when a stranger runs someone else's establishment.
- Supply. A bench of eight retirees has to be dense enough to reach homes in rural counties within 24 hours, so density in one cluster matters more than breadth.

title: Data Act Broker for Equipment Owners
one_liner: File and operationalize EU Data Act data-access demands so independent service shops can finally read the diagnostics that elevator, heat-pump, forklift and tractor makers lock away.
customer: Independent maintenance and service companies in the EU (starting with elevator/escalator maintainers, then commercial heat-pump installers, forklift and ag-machinery shops). They pay per monitored asset per month. Equipment-owning businesses (building managers, hospitals, logistics sites) are the secondary payer, because they hold the legal right.
problem: Original manufacturers use exclusive access to machine diagnostics and fault logs to keep 60-80% of the lucrative service market. Independents work blind, so they lose contracts to OEMs. The EU Data Act (applicable since 12 Sep 2025) gives the user of a connected product, including a business, the right to get the data the product generates. The user can also have it handed to any third party of their choice. In practice almost nobody exercises the right. The paperwork is unfamiliar, OEMs stall, and the data arrives in a different format from every vendor.
solution: An agency-plus-plumbing service. (1) Sign a user-authorization letter with the equipment owner. (2) Auto-generate and file the Article 4/5 access and third-party-sharing requests to each OEM and track statutory response deadlines. (3) Ingest whatever comes back, whether an API, a file dump or a portal export. (4) Normalize it into one cross-vendor schema per asset class. (5) Give the independent shop a fleet-health dashboard and fault-prediction alerts. Add a public compliance scorecard showing which OEMs comply, and escalate the ones that do not to national enforcement authorities.
why_now: The Data Act became applicable on 12 Sep 2025. On 12 Sep 2026, 16 days ago, its design obligation started applying to newly placed connected products, so data must be accessible by default. The right-to-repair movement is at peak momentum. OEM stonewalling now generates complaints that regulators must act on. No one has industrialized user-side requests yet, so the first mover sets the standard schema and templates.
revenue_model: Setup fee of about 50-150 EUR per asset for the request and integration work, plus 4-12 EUR per asset per month for the normalized feed and health analytics. Add-ons: predictive-maintenance alerts and a white-label owner portal. Later: sell anonymized cross-fleet reliability benchmarks to insurers and asset owners.
non_obvious_insight: A legal right is worthless until someone industrializes exercising it. The Data Act gives the data-access key to the owner, not the repairer, so the winning business acts as the owner's agent and sells the result to the repairer. The moat is accumulated request templates, OEM-by-OEM response knowledge, and one normalized schema. Every OEM refusal also becomes evidence for regulators, which turns compliance friction into marketing.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical and one country pair, for example independent elevator maintainers in Germany and the Netherlands, and reach them through trade associations. Retain a Data Act lawyer for a fixed fee to finalize request templates. Recruit 5 independent shops, get user-authorization letters covering about 50 units, and file the requests. Log every OEM response and format. Charge a pilot fee of about 1-2k EUR per shop for delivered data plus a first fleet report. Publish an OEM response-time tracker to build inbound demand. Expect uneven enforcement, so keep the pilot to OEMs that respond and use the ones that stonewall as regulator evidence.

Within those limits, I found no product that files Data Act Article 4/5 requests on an equipment owner's behalf, tracks OEM responses, and normalises the returns across OEMs for independent service shops. Every adjacent player is either an OEM platform, cars-only (High Mobility), farmer-facing (agrirouter), on-site diagnostics (Jaltest), or OEM-side compliance code (GitHub kits). Genuinely unserved: (1) the owner-mandate plus request workflow, (2) an OEM-by-OEM response and refusal log, (3) a cross-OEM schema for lifts, heat pumps and forklifts, (4) the independent maintainer as the paying customer.

Structural weaknesses to fix in the idea:
- No fixed response deadline. As I recall Articles 4-5, data holders must respond 'without undue delay'. I could not fetch EUR-Lex to confirm (its WAF blocked me), but the idea's 'track statutory response deadlines' looks wrong.
- Article 5(1) lets 'a party acting on behalf of a user' request data. The independent shop can therefore file the request itself with a signed mandate. The broker's moat is then normalisation and OEM knowledge, not legal standing. Model letters and the Commission FAQ (v1.4, 22 Jan 2026) will commoditise the templates.
- Article 9 lets OEMs charge data recipients reasonable compensation, with a cost cap for SMEs, so OEMs may bill the shops you serve.
- Only 'readily available data' is covered. OEMs will argue that diagnostics are derived data, or invoke trade-secret and security refusals under Article 4(6)-(8). Safety-critical elevators are the likeliest place for a security argument.
- Article 4(1) design-by-default applies only to newly placed products, and old lifts often have no OEM connectivity.
- Tractors and other ag machinery may already have sector-specific repair-information access rules under type-approval law (Reg. 167/2013, from memory, unverified), which weakens ag as a beachhead.

title: Independent Post-Reform Valuation for Medical Lien Funders
one_liner: A neutral, coder-signed valuation agent that tells LOP factoring companies and the lenders behind them what their medical receivables are worth after tort reform.
customer: Regional medical-lien funders and LOP factoring companies in Florida, Texas and Georgia that buy receivables from ortho, pain, chiropractic and ASC providers, plus the warehouse lenders and private-credit funds financing them. Buyer is the funder's CFO or head of underwriting, with the lender's credit analyst as the forcing party. First target list is 30-40 funders.
problem: Funders buy receivables at a fraction of billed charges, priced on attorney reputation and past collections. Reform changes the collateral. In Florida, 768.0427 makes the LOP, coded billing, the factoring purchase price and referral relationship disclosable and admissible, and amounts actually paid become the reference point. Cases accruing after March 2023 are only now reaching settlement, so the first post-reform collection cohort is landing on funders' books. Their lenders want borrowing-base reporting and independent collateral valuation, and no neutral standard exists. Carrier vendors, plaintiff platforms and data utilities serve everyone but the person holding the risk.
solution: Phase 1, fixed-fee 'Book Audit' in 10 business days. The funder sends a de-identified export (purchase price, coded bill lines, provider NPI, attorney, venue, dates, outcomes on closed files). Output: cohort-level expected collection and time-to-cash curves under current state rules; the top-decile at-risk receivables; a signed independent valuation letter the funder can hand to its lender or investors; and a 'bid sheet' of maximum purchase price by CPT bundle, provider type, venue and attorney tier. Phase 2: per-receivable scoring at purchase and monthly re-marking through a portal or API. Phase 3: lender-appointed valuation agent, where the warehouse lender designates and co-signs the engagement and receives monthly portfolio monitoring, like a collateral field exam. The coder bench and methodology from the parent are reused, but the output is a valuation, not a courtroom opinion.
why_now: First post-reform (Florida 2023) case cohort is resolving in 2026, so books are repricing now and lenders are asking questions. Private credit has moved into esoteric legal and medical receivables, and lenders in that class expect third-party collateral valuation. Florida's mandatory disclosure of factoring purchase price means every funder now knows its own buy price is evidence against the receivable, which forces a rethink of pricing and structure. LLM bill extraction makes coding a 2,000-line portfolio in days instead of months, with coder sampling for sign-off.
revenue_model: Book Audit $15-40k per portfolio, repeated semiannually. Subscription $3-6k/month plus $12-25 per receivable scored. Lender-facing monitoring $2-4k/month per credit facility, mandated by covenant. Illustration: 30 funders at $60k/year is about $1.8M, with upside from expanding to hospital-lien, workers' comp lien and pre-settlement receivables, and eventually independent collateral valuation for rated securitizations of medical receivables, where third-party valuation is mandatory.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody has looked at LOP bills as collateral. The same benchmark that is a weapon in a deposition is a valuation input in a credit agreement, and the buyer has the best data. Funders hold the only ground-truth set of what LOP bills actually settle for, by code, provider, attorney and venue, which carriers, defense lawyers and every vendor lack. Serving funders buys that dataset and tightens every later model. The issuer-pays conflict that damaged rating agencies is solved by making the lender the appointing party and by fixed fees, like an ABL field examiner.
first_30_days: Pull UCC-1 filings (for example the Florida Secured Transaction Registry) that name medical receivables or accounts as collateral, to identify funders and the banks and credit funds financing them. Recruit two coders, one ex-ABL field examiner or credit analyst who has run a borrowing-base review, and one part-time attorney to build a rules matrix by state. Run a blind backtest pilot with 2-3 funders. They send 200-500 closed receivables with outcomes hidden, we predict the realized collection, they compare. Offer it free in exchange for permission to use the calibration. Convert the best pilot to an $18-25k Book Audit and use the result to approach that funder's lender.

Stat. 768.0427 (https://www.leg.state.fl.us/statutes/index.cfm?App_mode=Display_Statute&URL=0700-0799/0768/Sections/0768.0427.html) already makes evidence of what was actually paid, or 120% of Medicare (170% of Medicaid where there is no Medicare rate), the benchmark for uninsured claimants. The fetched summary does not settle whether that applies to LOP treatment, so check the statute text. The defensible professional-fee benchmarks would come from Medicare multiples, payer transparency-in-coverage files or licensed data, not hospital files. | How this version avoids them: Enlyte and CLARA sell to carriers, and serving receivable buyers would create channel conflict with their own customers, so they rationally will not respond. EvenUp is plaintiff-side treatment and demand software and does not value receivables. FAIR Health and Turquoise sell charge and rate data, which we buy as inputs. JurisPro-style expert witnesses are litigation-only and have no portfolio product or lender-facing signature. The customer set is new to all of them. The parent's Florida commoditization problem disappears because the product prices collectability and duration, not a Medicare multiple, and our moat becomes proprietary realized-collection data plus the lender relationship.

title: Contingency Recovery for Contaminated Survey Sample
one_liner: A freight-audit-style recovery firm that finds contaminated and duplicated completes in the survey sample buyers already paid for, files credit claims against panel vendors, and keeps 25-35% of what it recovers.
customer: Wedge: mid-size full-service market research agencies (about 100-500 staff) that buy $1-10M a year of third-party online sample on fixed-fee client projects and absorb the reruns. Second wave: procurement teams at CPG, pharma and financial-services firms that already run recovery audits on freight, telecom and cloud spend but have never applied one to research sample.
problem: The parent idea asks insights teams to pay for a quality audit, and the research found no evidence anyone will pay $3-15k for one. Buyers do pay for money back. Kantar says post-field reconciliation (rejected sample) rates are up about 300% in three years, with some clients rejecting up to 40% of data (a vendor source). Contaminated completes that pass screening are paid for and used. The same panelist or device is also resold through several exchanges, so buyers pay twice for one human. Agencies eat the rerun cost, procurement never sees data quality, and nobody has respondent-level evidence strong enough to make a vendor pay. Vendors also fight individual rejections because their detector disagrees with the buyer's.
solution: Zero-upfront retrospective audit. The buyer gives read access to 12-24 months of respondent-level files, vendor IDs, invoices and MSAs. The firm runs LLM-assisted open-end forensics, cross-vendor duplicate detection (hashed device, IP and open-end similarity) and paradata review. It ingests detection flags from dtect, Verisoul or DQC where the buyer already has them. A 300-500-complete verified-human control cell per major vendor calibrates a population-level contamination estimate with error bounds. The firm then files claims for replacement completes, credits or refunds, citing the contractual quality clause. Claims argue that a vendor's batch exceeded the SLA (e.g. above 5% invalid, 95% CI) rather than fighting each flagged complete, which is where vendors dispute. Fee is 25-35% of value recovered, with no recovery meaning no fee. Stage two is prospective: a payment-hold or escrow layer where vendor payment for a batch releases after a control-calibrated pass, and a monitoring subscription.
why_now: Agents passing attention checks mean the largest share of contamination is now undetected at entry, which is exactly the paid-for-but-invalid pool that recovery targets. The cost stack collapsed: reading 10 million open-ended answers used to need human coders at dollars per complete, and LLMs now do it at fractions of a cent, so a contingency model works even on mid-size invoices. Pew's Aug 2026 study and NORC's fraud review give claim letters a public, credible methodology to cite. Buyers are already 'auditing suppliers, bringing sampling in-house and demanding accountability' (Greenbook), so procurement is primed.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 25-35% of recovered value. Illustrative unit economics, which are assumptions to test: $3M annual sample spend, 5-10% recoverable ($150-300k), 50% recovered, 30% fee, so $22-45k per customer per year. That is lower than the parent's $50-150k programmes but has almost no sales friction. Add-ons are a prospective monitoring subscription ($2-4k/month) and escrow at 1-2% of sample spend. Roughly 150-250 agencies and 30-60 enterprise buyers as a bottom-up serviceable market gives a $10M+ ARR business without ever selling 'quality' as a line item.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody budgets for data quality, but everyone has a process for accounts receivable. Turning 'is my sample clean?' into 'how much money are we owed?' moves the buyer from the insights head, who has no budget and no pain, to finance and procurement, who have both. The scarce asset is the same verified-human reference as in the parent, but used differently. It is needed only in small doses (a few hundred humans per vendor), which removes the 2,000-person panel problem and lets it be licensed instead of built. Population-level SLA claims also sidestep the detector-disagreement fight that makes per-complete rejections so contentious.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: post to insights and procurement communities and DM 20 agency founders and heads of ops. The offer is 'send one vendor's last quarter of respondent files, we tell you the recoverable amount, you pay nothing unless we recover'. Days 5-15: have a contract lawyer review 10 sample sample-vendor MSAs and SOWs to extract quality, replacement and dispute clauses, and draft a standard claim letter. Days 10-25: build the pipeline (open-end similarity, hashed-device dedupe across vendors, control-cell comparison) and buy 300 completes each from 4 major vendors as baseline. Days 20-30: sign 3 contingency agreements and file the first claim. Success is the first $50k recovered by day 90. Kill if, after 5 audits, recoverable value is below 2% of spend or vendors refuse every claim.
lineage: mutation of I0716 ('Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight. | How this version avoids them: Detection and scorecard vendors sell information or prevention: Verisoul, dtect, Roundtable, CloudResearch Sentry, ReDem and CleanID filter at entry, and DQC sells supplier benchmarks and a trust score. None recovers money already paid, and all are cheap enough to be input suppliers rather than rivals. Panel-owner stacks (Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, Pori) are the counterparty being claimed against, not a competitor. Verasight sells sample and could not credibly run claims against other vendors. The firm takes no referral fees from any vendor and never sells sample, so it stays neutral. Pew and NORC publish methodology free but never file claims. Traditional recovery-audit firms (freight, telecom, healthcare billing) do not touch survey sample, and the defensibility comes from the vendor-by-vendor claim-outcome database, which sets settlement rates and improves each claim.

title: Parcel-Level Rebuttals to Wildfire Insurance Scores
one_liner: Evidence packs showing a coarse satellite-derived wildfire score is wrong about one specific lot, filed under new statutory appeal rights.
customer: Independent insurance agents and HOAs or fire-safe councils in Colorado and California whose clients face nonrenewal or surcharges. Insurers' appeal desks are a later buyer.
problem: Colorado HB25-1182 (in force since July 1, 2026) makes insurers disclose the parcel's score, credit documented mitigation and offer an appeal. California AB 75, operative July 1, 2026, gives notice and dispute rights over aerial-imagery nonrenewals. But 'owners still have to prove their case', and many wildfire models lean on roughly 30 m fuel layers and stale imagery that misclassify irrigated, gravel-scaped or recently cleared lots.
solution: For each parcel, pull the disclosed model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density, distance to wildland) and overlay multi-date 15-50 cm satellite imagery showing vegetation change, roof material and clearance, plus dated homeowner photos. Produce a regulator-format rebuttal pack with a ranked list of cheap fixes, and give agents a dashboard that scans their whole book for likely score errors. The real edge is a growing database of which input errors insurers concede.
why_now: Both disclosure-and-appeal regimes went live in July 2026 and insurers' appeal desks are unprepared. Commercial constellations, including 30 cm Pelican and Vantor archives, plus 15 cm HD, have made high-resolution archives cheap. Regulators in CT, NH and PA say imagery alone is insufficient, and NY has a pending bill.
revenue_model: $149-$299 per parcel via agents. $10-$25 per parcel per year for HOA book scans. About $60 per appeal from insurers for standardised evidence intake.
non_obvious_insight: Wildfire scores are averages of coarse layers, so the cheapest way to change a score is often to fix an input error rather than harden the house. The resolution gap between 30 m models and 30 cm imagery is systematic, so a win on one lot tends to generalise to its neighbours and compounds into a book-level lever for agents.
first_30_days: Pick the Colorado Front Range. Recruit 5 independent agencies with 200+ WUI clients each, plus 2 HOAs. Run the first 50 score disclosures at a $99 pilot price per file, and track appeal success rate as the marketing asset.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: FireRisk.ai (RiskIntel AI), DefensibleHome Wildfire Insurance Survival Kit, Defensible Space Score (AACI Group / Five Bays Insurance Agency), Road Home Exteriors 'insurance-grade verification packets'. White space: Nobody found sells imagery-based, parcel-level, insurer-format rebuttal evidence, and nobody sells an agent or HOA 'scan the whole book for likely score errors' workflow. What exists is (a) free or $99 homeowner letter and template kits with no imagery (FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome, Defensible Space Score), (b) slow on-site certifications (IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home, Wildfire Partners), (c) contractor evidence packets sold with hardening jobs (Road Home Exteriors), and (d) carrier-side imagery scoring (Zesty, Nearmap/Betterview, Cape, Cotality, Verisk) with at most a compliance 'framework' for appeals. Specific unserved wedge: multi-date 15-50 cm imagery that shows a lot's actual condition (irrigated, gravel-scaped, recently cleared) against a 30 m coarse-layer score, formatted for Colorado's 10-day acknowledgement and 30-day decision clock, delivered to independent agents who carry many clients. Genuine caveats that shrink the gap: (1) The premise for California looks broken. AB 75's status page shows it 'held under submission' in Appropriations on 08/29/2025 and no source found shows it enacted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB75). The CA DOI's own report reportedly says there is no formal appeal process. So the 'statutory appeal right' in CA is unverified and Colorado is the only confirmed regime. (2) Colorado HB25-1182 (signed 28 May 2025, effective 1 July 2026, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1182) requires disclosure of the score, range and a plain-language explanation of features. It does not clearly require raw model inputs (fuel class, vegetation density), and it does not require insurers to accept third-party imagery. The 'pull the disclosed model inputs' step may be thin, and DOI enforcement is only that the Commissioner may request a copy of a denied appeal. (3) Insurers can satisfy the law with a manual mitigation discount, so a score correction may not change the premium. (4) Free and $99 substitutes cap willingness to pay for $149-299 per file. (5) Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality hold the same imagery and the carrier relationships, so the durable moat is the concession database, not the imagery.

title: Walkaway: PBM Offer Modeler Sold Through Associations
one_liner: A local-first tool that turns an independent pharmacy's own remits and invoices into a keep-or-drop answer for each January 1 PBM network offer, sold as a member benefit through state pharmacy associations.
customer: Wedge: owner-operators of 1-3 store independent pharmacies (roughly 40k-120k Rx a year) in one launch state, on PioneerRx, BestRx, Rx30 or QS/1, who have a 2027 network offer from at least one Big 3 PBM sitting on the desk. Buyer of record is the state pharmacy association (member-benefit license). Daily user is the owner-pharmacist plus their bookkeeper or accountant. Employers are not a customer at launch.
problem: Every Q4 an independent gets a take-it-or-leave-it PBM offer with about 30 days to answer, and the PBM implies that declining forfeits about a quarter of the business. The owner cannot answer two questions. First, what does this PBM's book actually earn per Rx after my real invoice cost and my cost to dispense? Second, what does walking away really cost in lost patients and front-store sales? The PSAO negotiates on the owner's behalf, but it is structurally conflicted (wholesaler-owned or fee-dependent; a hypothesis to verify in interviews). The alternative is an accountant with a spreadsheet at $150-250 an hour. Judges' and researcher's flaws this version fixes: the two-sided cold start (this version needs no employer and no pool to deliver value), the confidentiality and antitrust exposure (raw data never leaves the pharmacy), the missing evidence of willingness to pay (priced per decision, sold through a trusted channel), and a product that cannot be built from scratch before January (concierge first, parsers second).
solution: The pharmacy loads 12 months of 835 remits (or PDF remits, parsed on the machine by OCR and an LLM), its PMS dispensing export (Rx number, NDC, quantity, date) and wholesaler invoice lines. Everything runs in the browser or a local desktop app; nothing uploads. Output: (1) contribution margin per Rx by PBM, drug class and NDC, using true acquisition cost rather than NADAC alone, with underwater claims listed. (2) An offer model: enter the 2027 terms (MAC or NADAC-based schedule, dispensing fee, network fees, effective-rate true-ups) and the tool replays them on the last year's actual claims mix. (3) Walkaway math: patients on that PBM, refill-sync and front-store overlap, and retention scenarios (transfer, cash-pay, delivery) yield net annual profit if you sign versus decline. Sometimes the answer is that you make more money by dropping the book. (4) A one-page counter-ask with fee floors. (5) Opt-in give-to-get: contribute a k-anonymized summary (10+ contributing pharmacies per cell, 90-day lag, run by a third party under counsel's rules) to unlock peer percentiles. Guardrail: each pharmacy models and decides alone; the product never aggregates or signals intentions, which avoids group-boycott risk. The employer spread audit is a later output of the pool, not a launch product.
why_now: Today is late September and 2027 network offers are landing now, so there is a hard decision date. Closures (Rite Aid gone, Walgreens shutting about 1,200 stores) have made owners nervous and associations eager to show member value as membership shrinks. Browser-side OCR and LLM parsing of messy remits makes local-first onboarding a one-day job. A July 2026 open-source tool (rx-gap-finder, BestRx exports, runs client-side) shows owners will run this kind of analysis on their own machines, but it stops at spread by NDC. This would have been a consulting project in 2019.
revenue_model: Pharmacy: $299 per PBM offer analyzed, or a $749 season pass (all offers this cycle plus a mid-year re-check). Association: $8k-25k a year license for a member portal, co-branding and an aggregate state dashboard. Accountants and consultants serving pharmacies: white-label at about $1,500 per client. Illustrative bottom-up: 5 states x 300 paying pharmacies x $749 is about $1.1M, plus about $75k in association licenses. Ceiling on this product alone is about $13M (roughly 17-18k independents x $749), which is why the contributed pool is the platform for later index and employer-audit products.
non_obvious_insight: The product being sold is not a benchmark, it is a priced exit. Owners usually already suspect the rates are bad; they sign because they cannot put a number on walking away, and the PBM's 25% threat fills the vacuum. A credible walkaway number changes the negotiation and works with a sample of one, so it solves the cold start that kills two-sided data businesses. Second, local-first architecture is what unlocks the association channel: associations will not hold members' claims (liability, antitrust), but they will happily license a tool that never touches the data.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: 20 calls through one state association's executive director and board; ask directly whether the PSAO already offers contract modeling. Sign a letter of intent for a webinar and member email titled 'Model your 2027 offers.' Days 7-21: build 835 plus PDF-remit parsers for the three biggest PBM formats and PioneerRx and BestRx export mappers, and run the first 10 analyses by hand on screen share (free, in exchange for a case study and consent to use anonymized aggregates). Days 14-28: get a healthcare-antitrust attorney memo on data terms, the unilateral-decision guardrail and the aggregation thresholds. By day 30: 25 paid offer analyses ($299) and a $10k paid association pilot. Kill criterion: fewer than 8 of 20 owners say they would pay $299 to decide a live offer.
lineage: mutation of I1266 ('Pharmacy-Side PBM Ledger for Employers'), type: sharpened
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Truveris (truAudit / truGuard / Marketplace), Capital Rx (Judi Health), AffirmedRx, SmithRx. White space: Caveat on confidence: my WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before I ran any query in this session. The verdict rests on direct fetches of about 20 competitor and source pages plus GitHub searches, not on a broad landscape scan. It is a provisional 'gap', not a confirmed one.

What I did not find: no company that ingests pharmacy-side remits, benchmarks per-drug, per-PBM reimbursement against a peer pool, models Q4 network offers, and ties pharmacy-paid amounts to an employer's PBM claims file. The employer-side audit market is served: Truveris, benefits consultants, and transparent PBMs that market pass-through. Their audits appear to start from what the PBM hands over, and I found no sign they hold the pharmacy-paid half.

The pharmacy-side gap is plausible. PioneerRx, PQS and CPESN pages show no reimbursement-benchmarking or contract-modeling feature. Not verified: pharmacy services administrative organizations (PSAOs such as Cardinal, AmerisourceBergen Elevate, AAP, Health Mart Atlas) and pharmacy management system vendors may already offer contract review or reimbursement reports to members. - Getting employer PBM claims files with sponsor consent.
- Pharmacy remits are not uniformly 835 files.
- The January 2027 contract window is roughly 3 months away and cannot be met by a product built from scratch. | How this version avoids them: Truveris, Capital Rx, AffirmedRx and SmithRx sell to employers from PBM-supplied claims and never touch pharmacy economics; this version sells to pharmacies and does not compete with employer audits at launch (they become the later buyers of the pool's output). rx-gap-finder is a single-PMS hobby project (0 stars) that flags underwater NDCs; it has no offer replay, no walkaway math, no peer percentiles and no distribution, so it is proof of demand and a free top-of-funnel rather than a rival. PQS/EQUIPP does adherence and quality for star ratings with no reimbursement modeling, and CPESN sells clinical services to payers; both are potential distribution partners, not product substitutes. 46brooklyn publishes public price research, not per-pharmacy decision tools. The unverified threat is PSAOs and PMS vendors; the wedge against them is neutrality (no wholesaler or PBM revenue) and, if a PSAO already offers modeling, the fallback is to white-label the engine to PSAOs.

title: Supplier Watch: Customs Trails Plus Tool Census
one_liner: A supplier-monitoring subscription that reads US customs records for what your factory really ships and to whom, and upgrades to laser-tagged tool census and cavity-fingerprint forensics when the trail looks wrong or a divorce is coming.
customer: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50-500M revenue) with $200k-$5M of tooling in China (COO/VP supply chain, with general counsel). Secondary: small and mid-size importers re-sourcing to Vietnam, India, Mexico and Turkey, customs brokers, and factories buying verified credentials.
problem: Brands leaving a Chinese contract manufacturer rarely know which molds and dies they own, or whether the ex-supplier is still running them off the books. Importers of new suppliers can't tell a real factory from a shell. Customs rows tell you who ships what to whom but not what machines exist. A physical audit tells you what tools exist but is expensive and one-time.
solution: Tier 1 is a $2,500 remote 'Supplier Trail + Marketplace Overrun Audit': pull three years of import records for the supplier and its affiliates, find shipments matching the client's product descriptions and codes to consignees other than the client, compare volumes against the client's purchases and plausible capacity, and buy about 10 look-alike units from 1688, Alibaba and Temu to match against the golden sample and lot codes. Tier 2 is Tool Census ($6-15k per site) with a local partner, laser-tagging and cavity fingerprinting. Tier 3 is the forensic evidence pack and tool extraction. Tier 4 is a $149-499 per month watch subscription and a supplier-owned credential for smaller importers and factories.
why_now: Tariff pressure in 2025-26 is pushing brands to move production out of China within the last 24 months, and divorces put tooling at stake exactly when leverage is lowest. LLM parsing of shipping records and computer-vision matching of cavity marks are now cheap enough for a small team.
revenue_model: $2.5k remote audit, $6-15k per Tool Census site, $2-5k per month Overrun Watch per product family, $3-8k per evidence pack, 8-12% of appraised tool value on extraction, $149-499 per month and $150-400 per dossier for smaller importers, and $600-1,200 per year factory credentials. Expected first-year ACV for a manufacturer is $40-120k.
non_obvious_insight: The customs trail lets you run forensics remotely before anyone flies to China, since an ex-supplier shipping your part number to a third consignee shows up in the record as a shipper-consignee pair with volume. Conversely, every confirmed overrun case is a rare labeled positive for the anomaly model, which is otherwise unlabeled and generic like ImportGenius, and the census provides ground-truth capacity to sanity-check shipping volumes. The cheap watch subscription also identifies which suppliers are about to become the high-ticket cases.
first_30_days: Buy 12 months of import records for two categories and auto-build about 1,000 factory profiles, hand-auditing 20. Sell the $2,500 remote audit to 3 design partners through Ohio plant-manager and Reshoring Initiative networks. Line up a Dongguan or Ningbo audit contractor by referral and book an hour with an IP litigator who will white-label the evidence-pack format. Send 200 emails to sourcing managers and customs brokers for the watch subscription.
lineage: hybrid of I0552 + I1209 (Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics + Real-Factory Credentials From Customs Shipping Records). Why stronger: Tool Census alone is a high-ticket, low-frequency service with a long sales cycle, and customs credentials alone compete directly with ImportGenius, Panjiva and ImportYeti. Together, the cheap subscription is the funnel to the expensive census, the census and forensics supply ground truth that makes the credential defensible, and forensic cases keep improving the anomaly model.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Harris Sliwoski (China Law Blog), Alitheon (FeaturePrint), Red Points, Corsearch (Zeal 2.0, Investigations 360, Distribution Control). White space: Coverage caveat: the WebSearch quota (200 per session) was already used up when I started, so I could not run the planned 6-12 searches. I also could not check Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt, TechCrunch or open-source repos. The findings below come from about 25 direct page fetches, so treat 'nobody does this' as unproven. The vendors most likely missed are the many small China-based QC and sourcing agents that sell 'mold audits' and 'mold relocation', plus PI and investigation firms (Kroll-type). Do a manual pass on those before committing.

What I found: I found no productized, US-facing service that bundles (a) a serialized tool census, (b) cavity-level physical fingerprints, and (c) marketplace test-buy attribution of overruns to a specific tool. The problem is documented and treated as an unproductized legal-advice problem: Harris Sliwoski tells clients to keep an inventory form and audit quarterly, and never mentions a third-party vendor for it. Marketplace monitoring and takedown (Red Points, Corsearch, Alibaba's free IP platform) is commoditized and crowded. Object fingerprinting exists (Alitheon) but is aimed at electronics, aerospace and gray-market diversion, not tool-mark attribution.

Genuinely unserved: (1) cavity-level 'which tool made this part' attribution that holds up as evidence; (2) a tooling census standard for mid-market OEMs, timed to the exit window; (3) an evidence pack designed for counsel that a brand-protection vendor's screenshot-and-takedown workflow does not produce.

Weak points: Extraction (tool 3) is freight, customs and re-qualification work that sourcing agents and forwarders already do at low margin. Monitoring (tool 2, first half) is a commodity. Attribution is legally useful only when the overrun carries the client's IP (trademark, design patent, trade dress) and the client can enforce it. If the part is generic or unbranded, a match proves little. Chinese-court enforceability is unproven here. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ImportGenius, Panjiva (S&P Global Market Intelligence), Descartes Datamyne, ImportYeti. White space: The narrow wedge that appears unserved is a fixed-price, human-reviewed 'reasonable-care file' for a small US importer, sold through customs brokers. The SMB importer (Amazon or Shopify brand, or a $2-50M distributor) needs one factory checked before one PO. Enterprise tools (Sayari, Altana, Tradeverifyd, Trademo, Exiger) are sold by demo and are priced and scoped for large compliance teams. Data tools (ImportGenius, Panjiva, Datamyne, ImportYeti) sell rows and leave interpretation to the analyst. Inspectors (QIMA) and sourcing agents (Sourcify) sell physical checks, not a documentary file that maps to CBP's reasonable-care standard. The part I found nobody offering is a factory-claimed profile with consent-based buyer references, which is a two-sided credential. No visible player runs a supplier-owned reputation credential built on customs ledgers. However, the wedge is thin. (1) ImportGenius already markets 'supplier verification via shipping history' at the same $229-449/mo price band. (2) The raw-data floor is free or near-free. (3) Any one of Altana, Trademo or ImportGenius could add a 'transshipment risk report' feature quickly. (4) The factory-pays credential side has no demonstrated demand and needs a two-sided marketplace. Risks I could not check with the exhausted search budget: whether resale of licensed bill-of-lading data is allowed, that US import records often name the forwarder or trading company as shipper instead of the factory, that importers can request confidentiality under 19 CFR 103.31, and that no CBP safe-harbor exists for third-party dossiers.

title: Ride-Through Witness: Measure-First Large-Load Network
one_liner: Invert the parent's model-before-energization: ingest the UPS logs and power-quality waveforms sites already record, join them with grid-side PMU data, and auto-produce ISO-format ride-through and oscillation reports, growing into the reference data network that ISOs, OEMs and insurers rely on.
customer: Wedge: reliability and compliance managers and facility engineering leads at operators of 25-200 MW neocloud and colo sites in ERCOT and PJM, already energized or energizing. Second-side payers later are ISOs and TOs (aggregate feeds and model-validation reports), UPS and power-shelf OEMs (fleet analytics), and insurers.
problem: When a grid fault drops hundreds of MW of data center load, the ISO asks every site whether it tripped and why. The evidence sits inside the facility: UPS event logs, PQ-meter waveforms, power-shelf telemetry and transfer-to-backup thresholds. ISO PMUs only see the outside. As I read the reported 2024 Northern Virginia loss of about 1.5 GW, its cause was facility-side protection and backup-transfer behavior that grid operators could not see (verify against the NERC incident review). Pre-energization models are never validated against reality, and they decay as GPU firmware and UPS settings change monthly. Operators face blame, curtailment and NOGRR282 exposure with no forensic evidence and no ride-through margin figure.
solution: Software-first, with no hardware in the first release. 'Witness' ingests existing data (UPS event logs, PQDIF and COMTRADE files from existing PQ meters and relays, generator and BESS logs) and time-aligns it with public ISO and PMU frequency data. Within 24 hours of any event it generates an ISO-format disturbance report: what tripped, at what threshold and delay, how fast load recovered, and the oscillation signature. It also runs a continuous dashboard against NOGRR282 thresholds and detects GPU-cluster synchronized swings. Phase 2 adds a white-label certified point-on-wave recorder for sites without one. Phase 3 turns fleet data into measurement-validated models, a model-versus-reality score, OEM firmware benchmarks and an insurance risk score. We offer the report schema to ISOs and NERC as a standard, the equivalent of the IBR event-analysis and monitoring standards (PRC-028/029/030).
why_now: NOGRR282 has been in force since Aug 1, 2026, so the industry moves from modeling to operations, and the first real ride-through events at AI sites are being recorded now. NERC's IBR standards (PRC-028/029/030) show the regulatory template of monitoring plus event analysis for inverter-based resources, and it is plausible to extend it to large loads (unverified). GPU-load oscillation is now a public concern. Every operator already logs the data, and cheap cloud compute plus LLM-assisted log parsing make ingesting heterogeneous vendor formats cheap for the first time.
revenue_model: Operators: $30-70k per site per year for the subscription, or $10-15k per retro-analysis or event report. ISOs and TOs: $100-500k per year each for aggregated feeds and model-validation reports once 30 or more sites are connected. OEMs: $50-200k per year for cross-brand fleet analytics. Insurers: risk-score licensing. Data network effects and standard-setting are what make this a 10x outcome, with 300 sites at $50k as $15M in operator revenue alone, plus roughly the same again from the other sides.
non_obvious_insight: The 2024 event was an inside-the-facility information problem, and only the join of facility recorders and grid PMUs establishes causation. No single site sees aggregate risk, and only a neutral third party can pool data across UPS brands and operators, which OEMs and hyperscalers will not. That gives network economies and a cornered resource, proprietary as-measured behavior of real AI facilities in real faults. The parent sells the exam and this sells the proof you keep passing it. Free generic models cannot substitute for a fleet-wide, as-measured dataset. A retro-analysis of an operator's own past voltage dips is a sellable product with no OEM or pre-energization model required.
first_30_days: Sell a $10-15k Ride-Through Margin Audit built from an operator's own historical voltage-dip and UPS-transfer events, delivered by hand as a concierge service. Recruit one power-quality or protection engineer and one data engineer. Build parsers for PQDIF, COMTRADE and two or three UPS log formats. Contact reliability and compliance leads at 20 operators (ERCOT and PJM) and 3 TO or ISO planners, and offer a free report on one public event to each. Publish the draft report schema and an open primer on GPU oscillation signatures. Confirm what NOGRR282 requires in terms of operations-phase reporting.
lineage: mutation of I0996 ('Grid-Code Models for AI Data Centers'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Typhoon HIL (Data Centers solution), OPAL-RT (HYPERSIM, power-HIL), EPRI DCFlex, Emerald AI (Emerald Conductor). White space: Across this session's research I found no direct competitor selling packaged, hardware-validated large-load dynamic models (PSS/E plus EMT) with ride-through study reports and certification letters for GPU-cluster, PSU and UPS stacks. Nobody was seen selling OEM-level type-test certification for power shelves and UPS platforms. Adjacent players cover only pieces: HIL tools (Typhoon HIL, OPAL-RT), generic EMT consultancies, EPRI's flexibility consortium, workload-flex software (Emerald AI), and simulation software vendors with no data center library shown.

Three structural threats need answers:
1. Regulators and EPRI or NERC may publish free generic composite or EMT models, which commoditizes the model library.
2. OEMs (UPS, PSU, NVIDIA) own the confidential control details and may ship their own models.
3. Per-project EMT consulting already exists and is not verified either way for large loads.

The defensible white space is independent, hardware-validated, ISO-acceptable model packages and compliance evidence for the 25-500 MW neocloud and colo developers who lack in-house power simulators. It would be reused across sites through OEM platform type tests, not sold as bespoke studies.

Research limits: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before this task began, so competitor discovery relied on direct page fetches and GitHub search. Startup databases (Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt), news, and NERC or EPRI publication pages were not checked. Several NERC, EPRI and PJM URLs returned 404 or empty content. Treat the 'no direct competitor' finding as moderate-confidence. Verify manually against NERC LLTF outputs, EPRI data center model reports, and WECC or ERCOT model requirements before committing. | How this version avoids them: Typhoon HIL and OPAL-RT are pre-deployment lab and simulation tools. This is post-energization and field-measured. Emerald AI throttles and shifts load, and we measure and prove behavior. EPRI DCFlex runs nine demonstration sites and is a consortium, not a commercial fleet dataset, and it is a likely standards partner. Electranix, Danovo and Pearl Street sell project-based studies before energization. Hyperscaler in-house work is out of scope because our first customers are those without it. The unresearched risk is power-quality monitoring vendors, which sell hardware and generic dashboards. We ingest their files and become the analytics and ISO-reporting layer on top, and they may also be a hardware channel.

title: Satellite Witness for Neighbor Construction Claims
one_liner: A fixed-price, court-ready satellite-radar history of a condo tower's movement before and during the neighbor's pile-driving, sold through the plaintiff-side attorneys who represent Miami-Dade condo associations.
customer: Plaintiff-side construction and property-damage attorneys (start with about 25 Miami-Dade firms) who represent condo associations. The wedge buildings are barrier-island and downtown towers of 15+ stories in Sunny Isles Beach, Bal Harbour, Surfside, Edgewater, Brickell and Miami Beach that sit within roughly 200-300 m of permitted deep-foundation, dewatering or excavation work. The association's engineer and manager are co-users. Direct sales to boards come later.
problem: When a developer starts driving piles or dewatering next door, unit owners report cracks and vibration. The only pre-condition evidence is usually the developer's own visual crack survey, which is commissioned, held and dated by the party who may be liable. A sensor installed after work starts (SmartCore, about $20K at Marenas) has no baseline. A bespoke InSAR expert report from TRE or Fugro costs tens of thousands and takes months. The 2024 UM study found subsidence in 35 towers and tied some of it to nearby construction, so the fight is about causation: was the tower already sinking on fill, or did the neighbor's work do it? Without an independent baseline, associations either lose that argument or never file. This is a problem with a live trigger, a live adversary and a budget. It is not diligence the board has to be talked into.
solution: A permit-triggered evidence engine. (1) Monitor building, dewatering and foundation permits across Miami-Dade jurisdictions and auto-draw a 200-300 m influence zone around each site. (2) Process free Sentinel-1, OPERA DISP-S1 and ESA archive data into a retroactive per-building time series, so the baseline can be built after work has started. (3) Sell a $3,500 Causation Baseline Report: pre-construction trend, differential tilt across the footprint, and a difference-in-differences comparison against control towers on similar fill outside the zone. It ships with a hashed data package and a reproducible method note. (4) Sell $1,500/quarter Construction Watch, with a change memo each quarter. NISAR L-band corroborates it from June 2026 onward. (5) Provide a declaration and testimony through a contracted independent PE or geodesist, billed as pass-through. Everything is worded as a measurement of motion, never as a structural safety opinion. Work is structured as attorney-retained consulting.
why_now: The Dec 2024 UM/UH/GFZ study put construction-linked subsidence in Miami towers on the public record. Estructura's June 2026 Surfside-anniversary push has normalized InSAR for condos. Post-Surfside associations are hyper-vigilant and litigious. Florida courts apply the Daubert standard (since 2019), so a peer-reviewable, reproducible method matters. OPERA DISP-S1 (free since May 2025) and NISAR (public July 20, 2026) cut processing cost to near zero, while the expert-report incumbents still price as quote-based consulting. The Dec 31, 2026 milestone deadlines have boards hiring engineers who now ask about neighbors.
revenue_model: Per engaged association: $3,500 baseline, plus $1,500/quarter Construction Watch averaging 8 quarters, plus expert pass-through at cost plus 20%. That is roughly $16K in the first 24 months at about 80% gross margin before expert time. A $299/month Permit Radar alert feed for firms and property managers covers their client lists. Attorneys often advance evidence costs on contingency or hybrid matters and recover them in settlement, so the law firm is often the effective payer. Target is about 40 engaged associations in year one, or about $600K revenue, then repeat cases per firm (3-5 a year). Later, the same engine feeds the wholesale-to-engineers layer from the parent idea.
non_obvious_insight: The satellite is a disinterested witness that logged the building before anyone had a dispute. That means the baseline is built retroactively, at the moment of peak willingness to pay, which sensors physically cannot do. The parent's 'no moat, open-source' weakness becomes a strength here: in a Daubert setting the opposing expert can re-run the method, so credibility comes from reproducibility, chain of custody, the control-tower design and a growing record of accepted declarations. The buyer is not buying monitoring, which boards avoid. They are buying leverage: a $3.5K report that turns a multi-million-dollar claim from unprovable to provable. Attorney-retained work also blunts the parent's 'discoverable bad report' problem, since the client chooses whether to disclose (confirm with counsel).
first_30_days: Week 1: pull the roughly 50 active or pending foundation, pile and dewatering permits in Sunny Isles, Edgewater, Brickell, Miami Beach, Surfside and Bal Harbour. Compute influence zones (about 700 towers) and run the free Sentinel-1/OPERA stack. Week 2: contract one university-affiliated geodesist or PE as expert of record. Cold-contact 25 plaintiff-side construction and condo firms and 10 property managers with a named sample: 'the six towers next to [site] have moved X mm/yr since 2016, and here is the control comparison.' Weeks 3-4: sell 3 design-partner baselines at $1,500, convert 2 to Construction Watch, and get one attorney to write a methodology-review letter. Kill test: if fewer than 3 of 25 firms take a paid pilot, or the expert will not put a name to the method, stop.

This sells backward-looking, litigation-grade evidence through attorneys, triggered by a public permit event. TRE Altamira, Fugro, SkyGeo and NHAZCA sell bespoke quote-based expert projects at tens of thousands of dollars. This is a fixed $3,500 package with a pre-built method and a testifying expert on call. Sixense sells to contractors, who are the defendant side, so it is structurally conflicted here. OPERA is free but coarse and carries no chain of custody or expert. Domexa, CondoScan and CleanCondo have no physical-movement data. SatSense and Detektia are not in Florida litigation workflows. The defensible pieces are the permit-lead engine, attorney relationships, an accepted-expert track record and the control-tower dataset.

title: Contractor-First Road Billing, Then Repair Lending
one_liner: Invert the parent: sell to plow and gravel contractors who each serve dozens of handshake roads with a get-paid rail that binds every household to its share, then use the payment history and recorded covenants to become the lender for culvert and washout repairs no bank will touch.
customer: Wedge: independent plow, gravel and excavation contractors serving 15-80 private roads and shared driveways each, starting in one snow-belt county in Maine or NH. Later payers: road associations as borrowers, and community banks, credit unions and CDFIs as capital partners who buy participations in the loans we originate and service.
problem: A contractor plows a 12-home road on a verbal 'we'll split it'. He bills one neighbor, who fronts the money and chases the others. After one or two free-riders the fronting neighbor quits, so the contractor drops the road or absorbs the loss. Contractors also front fuel, labor and equipment for a season and are paid unevenly. When a culvert or bridge fails, a $30-150k repair has no borrower, since there is no entity, no assets and no financials. NC's post-Helene program (verified) demanded a 50% cost share, a single point of contact and proof of ownership, so roads that could not front cash and had no organization were shut out. Both sides of the road are cash-starved for the same reason, which is no legal counterparty.
solution: Phase 1, sold this October to be live by first snow. RoadPay for contractors: the contractor enters a road's seasonal price. Each household receives an e-sign Road Service Agreement (pro-rata formula, driveway-level opt-in, dispute rule) with autopay via Stripe Connect direct charges, so we never hold funds. The contractor gets one dashboard across all roads, automatic reminders and statements, and monthly payouts. Phase 2, winter: Season Advance. We advance 60-80% of a signed road's seasonal contract to the contractor, funded by a small credit line, and repay ourselves from the households' autopay through April. We underwrite at the road level using percent of households on autopay, contractor history and driveway geometry. Phase 3, year 2: Graduation. Roads with two clean seasons are invited to record an assessment-lien covenant (through the closing-rescue-style formation service), because it lowers their borrowing rate. Phase 4: Repair and cost-share bridge loans. $25-150k loans to the association for culverts, regrading and bridge repairs, repaid over 5-10 years from assessments, funded by CDFI and community-bank participation with us as originator and servicer. The same facility can bridge the up-front 50% of state reimbursement programs.
why_now: Winter 2026-27 seasonal contracts get signed in October and November, about six weeks from today. That gives a hard deadline and a full season of data inside a six-month window. Embedded payments are now a commodity (Stripe Connect handles onboarding, split payouts and money-movement compliance), which is the Wardley shift that makes a two-person team viable. Post-Helene aid design (verified) teaches that organized counterparties get capital and unorganized roads do not. Document extraction makes reading recorded covenants cheap enough to underwrite each road. Contractor cost inflation since 2021 plausibly makes non-payment more painful (hypothesis to test in interviews).
revenue_model: Phase 1: 4% of billings collected, paid by the contractor (no per-household fee, so the PayHOA $2 anchor never applies). Phase 2: 3-5% fee on advances, turned several times per season. Phase 4: 2-3% origination plus about 1.5% servicing on loans sold to bank partners, plus net interest on any retained slice. Illustration: 100 contractors x 40 roads x $3,000 is about $12M of billings, so about $480k of rail revenue. If 5% of roads borrow $60k a year, that is about $12M of loans and roughly $300-500k of origination and servicing. Early revenue is small. The business becomes large only if the payment history and lien-backed collateral become the standard underwriting file for private roads, which is the 10x claim.
non_obvious_insight: The party with the best data and the strongest incentive is the contractor, not the neighbors. He knows every road's parcels, who pays, and which culvert is about to fail, and one phone call reaches 40 roads. His invoice is a high-frequency touchpoint neighbors already accept, whereas a formation package is a rare, compliance-flavored purchase. The legal entity stops being a product and becomes collateral. Neighbors will sign a recorded covenant to cut their repair loan rate from, say, 14% to 8%, which they would never do for 'compliance'. It also removes the parent's conflict of interest, since the contractor is the customer rather than a party we take a procurement fee from.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 plow and gravel contractors in one county through local snow-removal and excavation groups, feed and hardware stores and Facebook groups, and offer free first-season setup on their 3 most annoying roads. Have an attorney spend $2-4k reviewing a generic Road Service Agreement and consumer-ACH disclosures. Build a no-code MVP in 2 weeks (contractor form, e-sign page, Stripe Connect autopay, manual reconciliation sheet). Convert at least 25 roads before first snow and measure the household sign rate (target 75% or better), autopay success and contractor willingness to pay 4%. Open a conversation with one CDFI or community credit union about a $250k participation for advances. Riskiest assumptions: whether households sign a contractor-issued agreement, and how to handle free-riders on a shared road, since the contractor can skip non-signers' driveways but not the common road. Also confirm lending and money-transmission licensing with counsel before Phase 2.
lineage: mutation of I0048 ('Private Road Associations in a Box'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Mainstream HOA and community-association platforms (Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC and similar), DIY legal templates and local real estate attorneys (Nolo, US Legal Forms, LegalZoom-style forms, local attorney drafting), Public alternatives: state road-association statutes and county road or special-assessment districts. White space: Tentative. Coverage was thin, so absence of a dedicated venture-backed product is not proven. What I found unserved:
1. No product I could find bundles the closing-triggered legal package (state-specific maintenance agreement, county recording, a lightweight entity) with the ongoing administration for informal neighbor groups. PayHOA covers dues admin generically and cheaply; the statutes and the law-firm and forms market cover formation; nobody stitches them together for the 5-60 home private road.
2. Competitively bid, pooled procurement of plowing and gravel across many associations. I found no tool for it.
3. Storm-damage documentation and an organized entity ready for state or FEMA private-road aid. NC's program required a single point of contact, ownership proof and a 50% HOA cost share, so unorganized roads were poorly placed to claim.
4. The transaction-channel distribution (attorneys, title agents and listing agents at a stalled closing) looks unowned by software vendors.

Weak points:

- The 5-8% procurement fee creates a conflict of interest. | How this version avoids them: PayHOA and HOA platforms: they sell to an association manager at about $2 per household, need an existing association, have no contractor side and no financing. Field-service and invoicing tools contractors use, such as Jobber-type products (from prior knowledge, unverified): they assume one billed customer, not 12 households splitting a road, and do not guarantee or advance payment. Group-payment apps like Venmo or Splitwise: no contract, no contractor payout, no recorded obligation. HOA lenders (banks serving incorporated associations, unverified): they require incorporated associations with financials, so tiny road groups are shut out, and we manufacture the collateral. DIY templates and attorneys: the legal formation is deferred until it unlocks cheaper credit, and delivered attorney-supervised. Maine statute and public districts: same, they are the legal substrate for the covenant, not a competing product. NC Private Road and Bridge Program: we bridge the cost share it demands. Local managers: potential partners for the lien-stage administration.

title: AI Exclusion Diff for Pro-Liability Renewals
one_liner: Forward a renewal quote or binder PDF and get, within 24 hours, a diff against the expiring policy, a breadth score for any new AI exclusion, and a client-ready gap letter. It is built for the professional-liability desk of independent agencies, and it also ranks competing quotes by exclusion breadth.
customer: The professional-services desk at independent agencies of 8-60 staff. That means the producer or account manager who handles 60-120 E&O, tech E&O, D&O, cyber and pro-services CGL renewals a year for architects and engineers, accountants, law firms, marketing and design agencies, and IT and software services firms. Much of their paper is surplus lines placed through wholesalers, which SERFF-based tools cannot see.
problem: AI exclusions on professional-liability paper are the broadest and most bespoke (Berkley's 'absolute' PC 51380, 'any AI' versus gen-AI only, vendor-supplied AI, BI/PD versus advertising injury, manuscript wording). They arrive buried in a stack of quote and binder PDFs, and the premium barely moves. The producer has about 10 minutes per renewal and no way to tell whether the exclusion is new, how wide it is, or whether it hits what the client actually does. Quandri and Zywave compare premium and limits. Patra checks 900+ points but is not AI-specific and does not diff against the expiring form. Filing trackers show what a carrier filed in a state, not what is attached to this client's policy.
solution: Intake is an email-in address with no AMS integration. The producer forwards the quote, binder or policy PDF plus the expiring policy. The output is a one-page report with five parts. (1) Diff: is an AI exclusion new, widened or unchanged versus expiring. (2) Breadth score of 0-5 across six dimensions: gen-AI only versus any AI, BI/PD versus advertising or personal injury, vendor-supplied AI, professional-services carve-outs, defence-cost treatment, and prior-acts effect. (3) A short 8-question client AI-use intake, which shows which of the client's real AI uses are now stranded. (4) A client-ready gap letter with a signed-acknowledgment page. (5) Quote-stage ranking: when the producer holds 2-4 competing quotes, it ranks them by exclusion breadth and drafts the exact carve-back request to send back, for example 'replace any-AI with gen-AI-only and carve out vendor-supplied AI'. Public filings (Trades Coverage, Certian, Gridex) are used only as a free auto-labeller for known forms. Delivery in the first months is LLM extraction plus a retired E&O underwriter reviewing every report. The output is a PDF plus JSON that files into Epic or Zywave as an attachment, so the product is a partner add-on and not a rival dashboard.
why_now: Renewals dated 1 Jan 2027 are the first big cycle after the ISO CG 40 47/40 48 forms and Berkley's absolute exclusion, and those quotes reach producers in Nov-Dec 2026, which is now. Trade press and associations (IA Magazine on 9 Sep 2026, Big I, Agents United) are telling agencies to review renewals for AI exclusions, but they give no tooling. Zywave's Advisor Agent, in early access since June 2026, is teaching agencies to expect renewal triage, and it does not read endorsements. Long-context PDF extraction on scanned binders is now cheap and reliable enough to do the classification at a cost of about $1 per document.
revenue_model: Pay per renewal at $150 for a standard quote diff and $450 for a multi-policy or manuscript diff. A $600/month plan includes 20 diffs. A $500 concierge audit on an agency's five largest accounts is the entry offer. Unit economics: about $1 of inference plus 15 minutes of reviewer time at about $60/hour gives roughly 85% gross margin on a $150 diff. This is my estimate: 1,000-2,000 US agencies run a real professional-liability desk, at 80 renewals a year that is $12-24k per agency, so 100 agencies is about $1.2-2.4M ARR. Referral revenue from affirmative markets is optional upside, and nothing depends on it, which answers the judges' doubt about the 10-15% commission.
non_obvious_insight: The thing a producer pays for is the ask, not the detection. Manuscript AI exclusions are negotiable, and a diff that says 'this wording is broader than the same carrier's competitor quote, ask for this replacement' turns a defensive letter into a shopping and negotiation tool that wins the account. The E&O-fear trigger also does not depend on the duty-to-advise law, which is weak in most states. Agencies that sell 'annual coverage reviews' assume a duty, and the signed acknowledgment turns that exposure into a documented file. The moat is not the public filings database. It is a labelled corpus of issued forms as attached to real quotes, including surplus lines, with outcome labels showing which carve-backs carriers actually granted. That corpus grows with every diff, and nobody can scrape it.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: recruit 10 pro-services-heavy agencies through LinkedIn and state agent-association contacts, and hire a retired professional-liability underwriter at 10 hours a week to write the 6-dimension rubric. Days 8-20: collect each agency's last 3 renewals for its 5 biggest pro-liability accounts (about 150 documents) and run the manual-plus-LLM diff. Measure the hit rate, meaning the share of renewals containing an AI exclusion the producer had not flagged. Proceed if it is 30% or more, and treat under 15% as the kill signal. Days 15-30: sell the $500 concierge audit and convert each agency to per-diff pricing for its live Nov-Dec 1/1 renewals. Publish the breadth scale v0.1 with 20 anonymised specimen forms as free content, and open a developer-partner conversation with Zywave and the Epic marketplace.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Patra (AI Policy Checking), Quandri, Zywave Apex / Advisor Agent, Testudo. White space: A real gap remains, but it is much narrower than the pitch. Nobody found sells a commercial-lines, broker-facing workflow that (1) takes a book's actual renewal forms schedules, quotes and binders (not just carrier-level filings), (2) detects and normalises AI exclusion breadth for each client, including bespoke wording such as Berkley PC 51380 and unnamed 'AI' language, (3) ties it to a 90-day renewal calendar, and (4) hands the producer a client-ready gap letter and a matched affirmative placement. This is a specialist quote-stage tool with a per-renewal price, and it could later be a partner or a buyer. Quandri is AMS-embedded and mostly personal lines, and its renewal review focuses on premium and coverage shifts. This is email-in and reads endorsements. Zywave Advisor Agent owns the 90-day trigger, and this product is the classifier it could plug in, not a competing dashboard. Testudo, Armilla, AIUC, Mount and Munich Re/Mosaic are carriers or coverholders with placement conflicts. This is neutral and earns nothing from placement. The free trackers (Gridex, Certian, Vorp Labs, ShadowLock) and Trades Coverage's 4,078-record dataset are carrier-level, so they cannot answer 'what does my client's quote say', and they become free inputs, not competitors. Rosella and FurtherAI do generic policy comparison with no AI breadth score, no gap letter and no negotiation ask. SERFF vendors (InsuranceFiling, Filing360, FilingRamp) sell to compliance teams, and their data misses surplus lines.

title: Cure Desk: Cash-Worker Packets for Health Centers
one_liner: A Spanish-first text-message case tool for health-center enrollment staff that turns a Medicaid noncompliance notice (or a pre-emptive look-back audit) into a state-formatted evidence packet for cash-paid workers, built on batch attestations from the crew leaders, landlords and households who pay them, billed per accepted packet.
customer: Enrollment and patient-navigation managers (certified application counselors, community health worker leads) at FQHCs and community health centers whose panels are heavy with day laborers, house cleaners, landscapers, roofers, temp-agency and informal restaurant workers, and street vendors. Narrow wedge: one Nebraska health center with a large Spanish-speaking panel (plus one refugee language), then a second state that verifies early. The end user is the patient in a 15-minute session with a CHW. The patient installs nothing and pays nothing.
problem: The parent idea was a self-serve wallet sold to MCOs. Judges flagged slow MCO procurement, weak enrollee adoption, and the IFR limiting plans to a support role. The competitor check found SteadyIQ and Emmy giving states free or bundled bank, payroll and gig linking, and Pointcare and Findhelp already holding the FQHC and MCO relationships. What none of them can serve is the worker with no digital trail. The IFR counts self-employment, gig work and in-kind work and lets people combine activities, so someone who cleans three homes for cash and helps on a landscaping crew is legally compliant but has no payroll record, no bank deposits to link, and a 30-day cure clock the day a notice arrives. Timing nuance: an HFMA summary of the IFR says self-attestation is allowed through 2027 (and once per beneficiary in 2028), so the documentation wall arrives in waves. Early-verifying states and audit-driven renewals come first, the general wall later. The first-year job is therefore both cure packets and building an audit-proof evidence file in advance.
solution: Six pieces. (1) Notice intake: the CHW photographs the notice, or the patient forwards it on WhatsApp or SMS. OCR extracts state, case ID, look-back months and deadline, and a 30-day countdown lands in the CHW queue. (2) State evidence rule pack: a maintained library of what each state and program accepts (in-kind work, combined activities, third-party statements, receipts), calibrated by logging every accept and reject reason. (3) Attester rail: the patient names who paid them, and that person gets a text in their own language ('Did Ana Ruiz work for you in August? About how many hours or how much did you pay? Tap to confirm'), creating a timestamped third-party statement in the state's format. Crew leaders, labor contractors, property managers, day-labor centers and church job boards get a batch screen that confirms 5 to 30 workers in one pass, with a reusable profile. (4) Packet: a PDF or portal-ready bundle with the hours or $580 computation, attachments and the patient's e-signature. The CHW submits as authorized representative, and the tool never decides compliance. (5) Outcome capture: accepted or rejected plus the caseworker's reason feeds the rule pack and billing. (6) Routing: patients who do have a digital trail are handed to the state's own Emmy or SteadyIQ consent flow, and exemption flags such as medical frailty are asked as a triage question only.
why_now: The June 3, 2026 IFR sets a Jan 1, 2027 start and a 30-day cure window, and six-month renewals for expansion adults begin around the same time (verify exact start), so notices and renewal checks multiply from Q1 2027. Nebraska is already live and is expected to move from self-attestation to verification. WhatsApp Business API, cheap OCR and LLM translation make a bilingual, photo-based intake cost cents per case, where a bilingual caseworker hour costs roughly $30. That is what makes a 15-minute assisted cure economical for a health center. In 2019 this would have needed a call center.
revenue_model: Per-case fee to the health center: $40 when a packet is opened plus $110 when the state accepts it (max $150, inside the parent's $50-150 range), with a $750 per month per-site minimum. Flat per-case fees rather than percent of Medicaid revenue keep it clean under inducement and billing-agent concerns (healthcare counsel to confirm). Channel revenue: white-label the packet builder as an API or module inside Pointcare, Findhelp or other health-center platforms at a 20-30% revenue share. Illustrative year-1 math (assumptions): 20 health centers x 40 packets a month x $120 average x 12 = about $1.15M. Later: a state-accepted-evidence data license to navigators and legal aid.
non_obvious_insight: Informal work is clustered behind intermediaries. One crew leader, property manager or household employer can attest for many workers at once, so each new attester makes the next patient's evidence nearly free, and the same attester serves patients at other health centers. The hardest segment for bank-linking vendors, where every cash worker is a costly manual exception, becomes the one segment with a network effect. The scarce asset is not the ledger but knowing what each state's caseworkers actually accept, which can only be learned by filing packets and logging outcomes. That data compounds with every case and cannot be bought or scraped.
first_30_days: Week 1: sign one Nebraska FQHC (or health center with a large Spanish-speaking panel) for a free concierge pilot, and call the state Medicaid policy office and two caseworker offices to ask which third-party statements are accepted as evidence. Weeks 2-3: build the flow from a Twilio or WhatsApp number, a Google Form, and a PDF template, with a bilingual attester text. Have the CHW enroll 25 real cash-paid patients and collect at least 40 attestations. Week 4: file the packets, or run the pre-audit in a state that is not yet verifying, and record acceptance rate and CHW minutes per case. Target: 60%+ acceptance and under 30 minutes a case versus 2+ hours today. Then take the numbers to a second health center and to Pointcare and Findhelp as a module partner.
